title: What makes vehicles go: muscles, fuels and electricity

summary.text: A cycle, a bullock cart, a bus and an electric scooter all travel down the same road. None of them moves by itself, so what is pushing each one? In this lesson you send a balloon rocket along a string to see how stored push becomes movement. You follow petrol back to tiny sea beings of long ago, and electricity back to the power station. You also compare city and village traffic, and work out real ways to save petrol and diesel.
summary.art: A road seen from the side with a cyclist, a bullock cart, a bus and an electric scooter in a row, each with a small picture above showing what powers it: a plate of food, a bundle of grass, a fuel pump and a plug.

intro.hook: Put a toy car on the floor and look at it. Wait. Does it go anywhere? Now do whatever you like to make it move, and say what you did.
intro.text: The car sat still until you pushed it, pulled it, tilted the floor or wound it up. Nothing with wheels starts by itself. Something has to give it a push, and the push has to come from somewhere. A real bus cannot be shoved along by hand. So what is doing the pushing inside it, and where did that push come from? Today you follow it all the way back.
intro.art: A toy car alone in the middle of a floor with a child lying on their tummy, chin on hands, staring at it.

outcomes: I can name what makes each of these go: a cycle, a bullock cart, a bus and an electric scooter.
I can say what a fuel is and name petrol, diesel and CNG.
I can tell where petrol and diesel come from, and why they will not last for ever.
I can say how an electric vehicle is different from a petrol one, and one reason it is not perfectly clean.
I can give five ways to save petrol and diesel.
I can compare the traffic in a city with the traffic in a village.
I can work out why a full bus uses less fuel for each person than a car.
I can test if more air makes a balloon rocket travel farther, and say what I found.

explanations.concept: No vehicle starts moving by itself: something must push or pull it
explanations.definition: A vehicle is anything made to carry people or goods from place to place. To start moving, every vehicle needs a push or pull from a source of energy.
explanations.description: A parked cycle stays parked. A boat with no wind and no oars only drifts. A bus with an empty tank will not start, however hard the driver turns the key. Every vehicle needs something to set it moving and keep it moving. Scientists call that something energy. For a cycle, the push comes from your legs. For a cart, it comes from a bullock. For a bus, it comes from burning fuel. For an electric scooter, it comes from a battery. The wheels and the body only carry and steer.
examples: A swing stops unless someone pushes it or you pump your legs.
A paper boat in a bucket moves only when you blow on it or stir the water.
A cycle going downhill is being pulled by the Earth, and you paid for that earlier by pedalling up.

perspectives.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker of the 4th century BCE
perspectives.explanation: A moving thing needs a push all the time, and it stops the moment the push ends. This fits a cart on a rough road very well, and people believed it for about 2,000 years.

perspectives.who: Galileo Galilei and Isaac Newton, in the 1600s
perspectives.explanation: A moving thing would go on for ever if nothing rubbed against it. On a real road, the rubbing of tyres and air slows it down. So a vehicle needs energy to start, and then more to make up for what the rubbing takes.

perspectives.who: The Vaisheshika Sutra of Kanada, chapter 5, composed in India more than 2,000 years ago
perspectives.explanation: Kanada wrote that motion begins from a push, a pull or a blow. He added that a moving thing carries a tendency, called vega, that keeps it going until something stops it. That is close to the later view.

explanations.art: A parked cycle, a still boat and a bus, each with a faded outline of a hand, a gust of wind and a fuel pump approaching.
explanations.context: This card sets up the question for the whole lesson: where does each vehicle's push come from?

explanations.concept: Muscle power: legs and animals have moved people for most of history
explanations.definition: Muscle power is movement made by the muscles of a person or another animal. The energy for it comes from food.
explanations.description: For most of history, going somewhere meant using muscles. People walked. They rowed boats. They rode horses and camels. They loaded carts and bullocks pulled them. Muscles are still at work everywhere. A child walks to school, a vegetable seller pushes a handcart, a cycle rickshaw driver pedals three passengers along. A muscle needs fuel too, and its fuel is food. Your breakfast is what moves your legs. The bullock's breakfast of straw and oilcake moves the cart.
examples: A person walks at about 5 kilometres in an hour and cycles at about 15.
A pair of bullocks pulls a cart with about a tonne of sugarcane at walking speed.
Dabbawalas in Mumbai deliver about two lakh lunch boxes a day using legs, cycles, handcarts and local trains.
explanations.one_view: That muscles move bodies using energy from food is measured in every study of exercise. How we should treat the animals who do this work has its own card.
explanations.art: A village road with a girl on a cycle, a woman pushing a handcart of bananas and two bullocks pulling a cart, a small plate of food drawn above each.
explanations.context: This card names the oldest source of push, which the board calls muscle power, and says its fuel is food.

explanations.concept: A cycle carries you farther on a plate of food than any other way of travelling
explanations.definition: A person on a bicycle uses about one-fifth of the energy that the same person uses to walk the same distance.
explanations.description: Walk one kilometre to a shop, and your body burns a little of your breakfast. Cycle the same kilometre, and you burn only about a fifth as much. Why? When you walk, your legs lift your whole body a little at every step and catch it again. On a cycle, the saddle holds you up and the wheels roll. Your legs only turn the pedals. In 1973 the engineer S. S. Wilson compared many animals and machines. For moving one's own weight a certain distance, a person on a cycle beat every animal and every engine he measured.
examples: You can cycle 5 kilometres and still feel fresh. Walking 5 kilometres takes an hour and tired legs.
A cycle weighs about 15 kilograms and carries a person of 60. A car weighs about 1,000 kilograms and often carries one person of 60.
India makes more than one crore bicycles a year, many of them in Ludhiana in Punjab.
explanations.one_view: The energy used in walking and cycling has been measured many times, and the result is not in dispute.
explanations.art: Two paths of the same length side by side: on one a child walking with five small idlis above, on the other a child cycling with one idli above.
explanations.context: This card gives a surprising number about the cycle and prepares for the question of saving fuel.

explanations.concept: Wind and flowing water carried boats for thousands of years before engines
explanations.definition: A sail catches moving air and a river current carries a floating boat, so wind and water can move vehicles without any fuel being burned.
explanations.description: Long before engines, sailors let the wind do the work. A sail is a big cloth that catches moving air. Indian sailors knew that the monsoon wind blows from the south-west for half the year and from the north-east for the other half. So ships left Kerala and Gujarat for Arabia and East Africa with one wind and came home with the other. Wooden ships called urus are still built by hand at Beypore in Kerala. On rivers, boats float down with the current. Wind and water are free. But they go only where and when they choose.
examples: The English word 'catamaran' comes from the Tamil kattumaram, a boat of logs tied together.
A paper boat in a gutter after rain is carried by the water with no push from you.
The seeds of a silk-cotton tree ride the wind on fluff, with no fuel at all.

perspectives.who: A Greek sailors' guide of the 1st century CE, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
perspectives.explanation: It says a Greek pilot named Hippalus discovered how to cross the open sea to India on the monsoon wind.

perspectives.who: Historians of the Indian Ocean, such as Lotika Varadarajan
perspectives.explanation: Indian, Arab and East African sailors were crossing on the monsoon long before any Greek ship came. The Greek book records the moment when Greeks learned of it, and not the moment of discovery.

explanations.art: A wooden uru with a full sail crossing a blue sea, with curved arrows for the south-west and north-east monsoon winds.
explanations.context: This card shows two sources of push that need no fuel, and credits the sailors who mastered the monsoon.

explanations.concept: A fuel is something that gives out heat when it burns
explanations.definition: A fuel is a material that releases stored energy as heat when it burns. Petrol, diesel, CNG, cooking gas, coal and wood are fuels.
explanations.description: Light a diya, and the oil slowly disappears while the flame gives light and warmth. The oil is a fuel, because burning it gives out heat. Wood, coal, kerosene and cooking gas are fuels. Most vehicles on the road burn one of three. Petrol is a thin liquid that catches fire very easily, and it is used in scooters and many cars. Diesel is a thicker, oily liquid, used in buses, lorries and tractors. CNG is a gas squeezed tightly into a strong cylinder, used in many autos and city buses. Burning also needs air.
examples: A candle under an upturned tumbler goes out in a few seconds, because the air inside is used up. An engine needs a steady supply of air for the same reason.
A petrol pump has separate nozzles for petrol and diesel. Putting the wrong one in a vehicle spoils the engine.
Aeroplanes burn a fuel much like kerosene. Big ships burn a thick, tarry oil.
explanations.one_view: What counts as a fuel and what burning needs are agreed chemistry.
explanations.art: Three containers in a row: a clear bottle of pale petrol, a bottle of yellowish diesel and a green CNG cylinder, with a small flame above each.
explanations.context: This card says what a fuel is and names the three road fuels the board lists.

explanations.concept: An engine burns fuel in a closed space, and the hot gas pushes the wheels round
explanations.definition: An engine is a machine that turns the heat from burning fuel into movement. In a vehicle engine, fuel burns inside closed tubes called cylinders and the expanding hot gas pushes a piston.
explanations.description: Inside an engine are metal tubes called cylinders. In each tube sits a metal plug that can slide, called a piston. A tiny spray of fuel and some air go into the tube. A spark sets them alight. The burning makes very hot gas, and hot gas needs far more room. It shoves the piston down hard. This happens many times a second. Rods and gears turn those shoves into the spinning of the wheels. But most of the heat never reaches the wheels. In a petrol car, only about a quarter of the fuel's energy moves the car. The rest warms the engine and the air.
examples: The bonnet of a car that has just been driven is hot to stand near. That warmth is fuel that did no pushing.
The 'dug-dug-dug' of a motorcycle is the sound of fuel burning in the cylinder, one small bang after another.
A pressure cooker's whistle is lifted by hot steam that needs more room. A steam engine uses the same push.
explanations.one_view: How an engine works, and how much of the fuel's energy it wastes as heat, are measured by engineers and not disputed.
explanations.art: A cut-away of one engine cylinder in two steps: fuel and air with a spark, and then a burst of hot gas pushing the piston down, joined by a rod to a turning wheel.
explanations.context: This card explains how burning becomes movement, and shows that an engine wastes most of its fuel as heat.

explanations.concept: Petrol and diesel come from oil under the ground, made from tiny sea beings of long ago
explanations.definition: Petrol and diesel are made from petroleum, a thick dark oil found deep underground. Petroleum formed over millions of years from the buried remains of tiny beings that lived in ancient seas. Coal formed from ancient forests. These are called fossil fuels.
explanations.description: Where does petrol come from? Many people think of dinosaurs. The real answer is smaller and stranger. Long before the dinosaurs, and during their time, warm seas were full of tiny floating beings, too small to see. When they died, they sank into the mud. More mud covered them. Over millions of years the layers were squeezed and heated deep underground. The remains slowly turned into a thick dark oil called petroleum, and into gas. Today people drill deep wells to bring up the oil. At a factory called a refinery it is separated into petrol, diesel, kerosene, cooking gas and tar.
examples: India's first oil well was drilled at Digboi in Assam in about 1889, and oil is still pumped there.
Bombay High, an oil field under the sea west of Mumbai, has been worked since the 1970s.
India finds only a small part of the oil it uses. About 85 out of every 100 litres come by ship from other countries.
The black tar on a road is the thickest part of the same oil.
explanations.one_view: Almost all scientists who study rocks agree on this origin. A small group has argued otherwise, and their case is given under the views that challenge.
explanations.art: A slice through the Earth in three panels: tiny beings floating in an ancient sea, layers of mud pressing down, and an oil well today reaching a dark pool.
explanations.context: This card follows petrol and diesel back to their source and corrects the common belief that oil is made from dinosaurs.

explanations.concept: Fossil fuel is very old sunlight, and we burn it far faster than it was made
explanations.definition: The energy in fossil fuels was first caught from sunlight by living beings millions of years ago. These fuels take millions of years to form, so the amount that can be taken from the Earth is limited.
explanations.description: Those tiny sea beings lived on sunlight, as green plants do today. They caught the Sun's energy and stored it in their bodies. When their remains became oil, the stored energy stayed. So when an engine burns petrol, the heat that comes out is sunlight that fell on a sea millions of years ago. The oil took millions of years to make. People began burning it in large amounts only a century and a half ago. Nobody can make more. That is the first reason to use petrol and diesel carefully. One honest note: science can measure energy exactly, but has no final answer to what energy is.
examples: The grass a bullock eats caught its sunlight this season. The diesel in a tractor caught its sunlight before there were any people.
A piece of coal sometimes shows the print of a leaf from a forest of about 30 crore years ago.
The world burns about 10 crore barrels of oil every single day. A barrel holds nearly 160 litres.

perspectives.who: Geologists such as M. King Hubbert, who warned in 1956 that oil would run short
perspectives.explanation: The oil that is easy to reach will be used up, and what is left will cost much more to get. He predicted that oil from American wells would begin to fall by about 1970, and it did for several decades.

perspectives.who: Economists such as Morris Adelman
perspectives.explanation: New methods keep finding and reaching more oil. The world will stop burning oil because of the harm it does and because better things replace it, long before the last drop is gone.

explanations.art: A long sunbeam drawn as a ribbon that passes through an ancient sea, down into dark rock, up an oil well, into a petrol pump and out of a scooter as a small glow.
explanations.context: This card explains why fossil fuels are limited, which is the first reason for saving them.

explanations.concept: Burning one litre of petrol puts more than two kilograms of an unseen gas into the air
explanations.definition: When fuel burns, it joins with oxygen from the air and forms carbon dioxide, an invisible gas that traps heat around the Earth. Burning one litre of petrol produces about 2.3 kilograms of carbon dioxide.
explanations.description: Burning does not make the fuel vanish. It joins with a part of the air called oxygen and becomes new gases. The main one is carbon dioxide. You cannot see or smell it. A litre of petrol weighs less than a kilogram, yet burning it makes about 2.3 kilograms of carbon dioxide. The extra weight is oxygen taken from the air. Carbon dioxide spreads through the sky and holds in heat, like a blanket. More of it means a warmer Earth. Exhaust pipes also give out soot and gases that hurt lungs. That is the second reason to save fuel.
examples: Look at the edge of a busy road, or under a flyover. A dark grey film there is often soot from exhaust pipes. Look only, and never touch it.
On a busy road your eyes sting. In the open country they do not.
A car that runs 15 kilometres on a litre puts out close to 150 grams of carbon dioxide for every kilometre.

perspectives.who: Eunice Foote, an American scientist, in 1856
perspectives.explanation: She filled glass tubes with different gases and stood them in the sun. The tube of carbon dioxide grew hottest and stayed hot longest. She wrote that an atmosphere of this gas would give the Earth a higher temperature. Her work was forgotten for a hundred and fifty years.

perspectives.who: Svante Arrhenius, a Swedish scientist, in 1896
perspectives.explanation: He worked out how much the Earth would warm if the carbon dioxide in the air doubled. He thought it would take thousands of years and might be pleasant. Burning has grown so fast that the doubling may come in two or three centuries from the 1850s, far sooner than he thought.

explanations.art: A balance scale with a one-litre bottle of petrol on one side and, on the other, a much heavier grey cloud marked '2.3 kg', with small arrows of oxygen flowing into the cloud.
explanations.context: This card says what comes out of an exhaust pipe and why it matters, with a number that surprises most adults.

explanations.concept: CNG is a cleaner-burning gas, and Delhi's buses and autos switched to it by 2002
explanations.definition: CNG, compressed natural gas, is mostly a gas called methane, squeezed into strong cylinders. It burns with much less soot than diesel.
explanations.description: Natural gas is found underground, often together with oil. It is squeezed until a great deal fits in a cylinder, and it is then called CNG. Look for a green or yellow auto or bus with 'CNG' painted on it. This gas burns with almost no black smoke. In the 1990s Delhi's air was thick with diesel soot. A lawyer, M. C. Mehta, took the matter to the Supreme Court. Scientists and writers at the Centre for Science and Environment, led by Anil Agarwal and Sunita Narain, gathered the evidence. The court ordered every bus, auto and taxi in Delhi to switch. By the end of 2002 they had.
examples: A CNG bus pulling away from a stop leaves no black cloud behind.
CNG is still a fossil fuel. Burning it makes carbon dioxide, though somewhat less than petrol or diesel for the same journey.
Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Pune and many other cities now run autos and buses on CNG.

perspectives.who: The Centre for Science and Environment, and studies soon after the switch
perspectives.explanation: Soot and some harmful gases in Delhi's air fell in the first years after 2002. It showed that a city can change its fuel in a few years when it decides to.

perspectives.who: Researchers who measured Delhi's air in later years, such as Sarath Guttikunda
perspectives.explanation: The gain was soon swallowed. The number of private cars and two-wheelers kept rising, and smoke from lorries, dust, factories and burning waste grew as well. A cleaner fuel helps, and it cannot make up for many more vehicles.

explanations.art: A Delhi street with a green CNG bus and a green-and-yellow auto, clear air behind them, and a faded picture of an old bus trailing black smoke.
explanations.context: This card explains the third road fuel and tells how citizens, scientists and a court changed a city's fuel.

explanations.concept: An electric vehicle has a battery and a motor in place of a fuel tank and an engine
explanations.definition: An electric vehicle stores electrical energy in a battery. An electric motor uses magnets to turn that energy directly into the spinning of the wheels, without burning anything.
explanations.description: An electric scooter has no fuel tank and no exhaust pipe. It carries a battery, which is a store of electricity like the one in a phone, only far bigger. Wires take the electricity to a motor. Inside a motor, electricity makes magnets push and pull each other, and this turns a rod round and round. Nothing burns, so the motor is quiet and stays fairly cool. It wastes little. More than three-quarters of the battery's energy reaches the wheels. When the battery is empty, it is filled again from a plug. That takes far longer than filling a tank.
examples: Stand beside an electric auto as it starts. You hear a soft whine and no rattle.
A ceiling fan, a mixer and a toy car all have electric motors inside.
India's first electric car, the Reva, was built in Bengaluru in 2001 by Chetan Maini's company.
E-rickshaws, which run on batteries, now carry crores of short rides in Indian towns every day.
explanations.one_view: How a battery and a motor work is agreed engineering. How clean an electric vehicle is, taken as a whole, is argued over, and the card after next takes it up.
explanations.art: A see-through electric scooter showing a flat battery under the footboard, a wire, and a round motor in the back wheel, with a plug and cable beside it.
explanations.context: This card explains how electricity moves a vehicle and how that differs from burning fuel.

explanations.concept: Electric cars are older than petrol cars, and they lost the first race
explanations.definition: Battery-powered carriages were built from the 1830s. In the year 1900 more electric cars than petrol cars were made in the USA.
explanations.description: Most people think the electric car is a new invention. It is older than the petrol car. Inventors built small carriages run by batteries in the 1830s. By 1900 electric taxis worked in New York and London. They were quiet and clean and needed no cranking to start. In that year American factories made more electric cars than petrol cars. They made even more steam cars than either. Then petrol won. Oil was found in huge amounts and became cheap. A petrol tank took a car much farther than the heavy batteries of that time could. For a hundred years the electric car was almost forgotten.
examples: Milk was delivered by quiet electric vans in British cities for most of the 1900s.
In 2019 the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino. They made the light, strong lithium battery that brought electric vehicles back.
Electric trains never went away. Mumbai's first electric train ran in 1925.
explanations.one_view: The production figures for 1900 and the dates of early electric vehicles are on record. This card is here to show that which machine wins depends on prices and discoveries as well as on which is better.
explanations.art: A street scene of about 1900 with a tall, boxy electric taxi beside a horse carriage, and a modern electric car drawn faintly in the same pose.
explanations.context: This card pushes against the idea that electric vehicles are new, and shows that history could have gone another way.

explanations.concept: Is an electric vehicle clean? It depends on where the electricity comes from and how the battery is made
explanations.definition: An electric vehicle gives out no exhaust on the road. How clean it is overall depends on how its electricity is made and how its battery is mined and built.
explanations.description: An electric scooter has no smoke coming out of it. But the electricity in its battery was made somewhere. In India about seven units of electricity in every ten come from burning coal at power stations. So some smoke has only moved, from the street to a chimney far away. The battery needs metals such as lithium and cobalt, which are dug from mines. Much of the world's cobalt comes from the Congo in Africa, where some mines are dangerous and children have been found working in them. So is an electric vehicle better? Most careful studies say yes, by a modest amount today and by more in future. Not everyone agrees on how much.
examples: An electric scooter charged from solar panels on a roof in the daytime is running on that day's sunlight.
City air gets cleaner where people breathe it, even when the power station still burns coal.

perspectives.who: The International Council on Clean Transportation, in a study led by Georg Bieker in 2021
perspectives.explanation: Counting everything from mine to scrapyard, an electric car in India caused about a fifth to a third less warming gas than a petrol car. The gap will widen as India builds more solar and wind power.

perspectives.who: Critics such as the energy writer Vaclav Smil
perspectives.explanation: Mining, heavy batteries and coal power take away much of the gain. Replacing a billion engines with a billion batteries leaves the real problem, which is too many heavy vehicles.

perspectives.who: People who live near the mines, and groups such as Amnesty International in a report of 2016
perspectives.explanation: The cleaner air of rich cities is paid for by miners and villages elsewhere. A fair change must count their health and their land as well.

explanations.art: An electric scooter plugged into a wall, with the wire continuing as a long dotted line to a coal power station with a smoking chimney on one side and a field of solar panels on the other.
explanations.context: This card gives the honest debate about electric vehicles, so the child does not take 'electric' to mean 'harmless'.

explanations.concept: Fuel from plants: ethanol in petrol, and the argument over food or fuel
explanations.definition: Ethanol is a liquid fuel made by fermenting the sugar or starch of plants such as sugarcane, maize and rice. In India it is mixed into petrol.
explanations.description: Fuel can be grown. Sugarcane juice is left for tiny beings called yeast to feed on. They turn the sugar into a liquid that burns, called ethanol. Since 2025, about one-fifth of the petrol sold at most Indian pumps has been ethanol. The good side is that the plants caught their sunlight this year, and new plants grow next year. India also buys less oil from abroad. But there is another side. Sugarcane is a very thirsty crop. And land, water and grain used for fuel are not being used for food.
examples: A sticker on many petrol pumps reads 'E20', meaning 20 parts ethanol in every 100.
Brazil began a national ethanol programme in 1975. Many Brazilian cars now run on ethanol, on petrol, or on any mix of the two.
Rudolf Diesel showed one of his first engines running on groundnut oil at a fair in Paris in 1900.

perspectives.who: The Government of India and NITI Aayog, in the ethanol plan of 2021
perspectives.explanation: Blending ethanol saves foreign money, gives farmers a second buyer for their crop and reduces some harmful exhaust gases.

perspectives.who: Water and food researchers, such as the economist Ashok Gulati
perspectives.explanation: Growing the sugarcane for one litre of ethanol takes thousands of litres of water, in states that are already short of it. Using rice and maize for fuel can push up the price of food for the poor.

perspectives.who: Engineers working on ethanol from farm waste
perspectives.explanation: Ethanol can also be made from straw, husks and stalks left after harvest, which nobody eats. This is harder and costlier today. If it can be made cheaply, the quarrel between food and fuel goes away.

explanations.art: A field of sugarcane with a path splitting in two, one branch leading to a plate of food and a block of jaggery, the other to a petrol pump marked E20.
explanations.context: This card shows a fuel that can be grown again, and a real disagreement about using it.

explanations.concept: A full bus uses far less fuel for each person than a car or scooter
explanations.definition: Fuel use per person is the fuel a vehicle burns divided by the number of people it carries. A vehicle with many passengers shares its fuel among them.
explanations.description: A city bus is a thirsty machine. It goes only about 4 kilometres on a litre of diesel, while a car goes about 15. So is the car better? Count the people. If the bus carries 50 people, that one litre has moved 50 people 4 kilometres. That is the same as moving one person 200 kilometres. The car with only its driver has moved one person 15 kilometres. The bus is more than ten times better. Fill the car with four people and it improves to 60. Trains and metros do better still. Sharing is the biggest fuel saver there is.
examples: A scooter that goes 45 kilometres on a litre and carries two people has moved one person 90 kilometres on that litre.
A school bus with 40 children replaces 40 separate trips by car or scooter.
An empty bus is worse than a car. Sharing saves fuel only when the seats are filled.
explanations.one_view: This is arithmetic on measured fuel figures. The figures change with the vehicle and the traffic, and the comparison holds across the usual range.
explanations.art: A bar chart drawn as roads of different lengths: a short road for a car with one person (15), a longer road for a car with four (60), a longer one for a scooter with two (90), and the longest for a bus with fifty (200).
explanations.context: This card does the sum that shows why sharing rides saves fuel, which the board asks children to suggest.

explanations.concept: Ways to save petrol and diesel: fewer trips, shared trips and gentle driving
explanations.definition: Saving fuel means getting the same travel done while burning less. It can be done by avoiding engine trips, by sharing vehicles and by using each vehicle carefully.
explanations.description: There are three kinds of saving. First, do not burn fuel at all: walk or cycle for short trips, and do three errands in one outing in place of three. Second, share: take the bus, train or metro, use the school bus, or travel with neighbours going the same way. Third, drive with care. Switch off the engine at a long red light or a railway gate. Keep the tyres pumped up, because soft tyres drag. Drive at a steady 45 to 55 kilometres an hour without sudden racing and braking. Have the engine serviced. Do not carry loads you do not need.
examples: A car standing with the engine running burns roughly half a litre to one litre of petrol in an hour and goes nowhere.
At a closed railway gate, count how many drivers switch off and how many keep the engine running.
A shop 500 metres away is six or seven minutes on foot. Starting a cold engine for that trip uses extra fuel.
India's Petroleum Conservation Research Association has taught these tips to drivers since 1978.
explanations.one_view: Each of these has been measured by engineers and is agreed. Whether saving by each driver adds up to saving by the whole country is a harder question, and the next card asks it.
explanations.art: Three panels: a family walking to a nearby shop with a cloth bag, children boarding a school bus, and a scooter at a railway gate with its engine off and a tyre being pumped.
explanations.context: This card delivers the board point of suggesting ways to save petrol and diesel, grouped so that they are easy to remember.

explanations.concept: When engines waste less fuel, people often travel more: the saving that gets eaten
explanations.definition: The rebound effect is the tendency for people to use more of something when it becomes cheaper to use. Better engines lower the cost of each kilometre, which can lead to more driving and larger vehicles.
explanations.description: Here is a puzzle. Engines today get much more out of a litre than engines fifty years ago. Yet the world burns more petrol and diesel than ever. How can that be? In 1865 an English thinker, William Stanley Jevons, noticed the same thing with coal. Steam engines had been made far more saving. Coal use went up, not down. Cheaper running meant that people built more engines and used them more. The same has happened on the roads. When each kilometre costs less, people drive farther and buy bigger vehicles. So better machines alone may not save fuel.
examples: Cars sold in India have grown taller and heavier over twenty years, even as their engines improved.
A family that buys a scooter after years of cycling may make trips it never made before.

perspectives.who: William Stanley Jevons, in 'The Coal Question', 1865
perspectives.explanation: It is a confusion of ideas to suppose that using a fuel more efficiently leads to using less of it. The very opposite is the truth. Efficiency makes a fuel more useful, so more is wanted.

perspectives.who: Energy researchers such as Steve Sorrell, in a review of 2007
perspectives.explanation: The rebound is real but usually partial. For cars, something like a tenth to a third of the saving is eaten by extra driving. The rest is a true saving, so better engines are still worth having.

perspectives.who: Many economists
perspectives.explanation: A better engine alone is not enough. Saving comes when it is joined with a limit, such as a fuel tax or fewer parking spaces. Good buses also help, because they make people choose not to drive.

explanations.art: A small old car with a thick fuel pipe driving a short road, and beside it a big new car with a thin fuel pipe driving a road three times as long, the two fuel cans at the end the same size.
explanations.context: This card questions the easy idea that better machines save fuel, with a debate that began in 1865.

explanations.concept: City traffic and village traffic are different in number, kind, speed and noise
explanations.definition: Traffic is all the vehicles and people moving on roads. A city has many more vehicles in a small space than a village, and a different mix of them.
explanations.description: Stand at a city crossing for five minutes. You may count hundreds of vehicles: cars, scooters, autos, buses, lorries, perhaps a metro train overhead. There are signals, flyovers, horns, and often a jam. Now stand on a village road. In the same five minutes you may count only about ten. They might be a tractor, a shared auto, two motorcycles, some cycles, a bullock cart and a bus that comes four times a day. People walk in the road and animals cross it. The air is clearer and you can hear birds. But the school, the market or the hospital may be many kilometres away, with few ways to reach them.
examples: India has more than 30 crore registered motor vehicles, and about three in every four are two-wheelers.
In Bengaluru in 2023, a trip of 10 kilometres took about 28 minutes on average. That is a speed of only about 21 kilometres an hour.
In many villages one jeep or shared auto carries schoolchildren, milk cans and vegetable sacks in the same trip.
At harvest time a village road fills with tractors and loaded carts, and for a few weeks it has a rush hour of its own.

perspectives.who: City dwellers and city planners
perspectives.explanation: Cities have many choices: buses every few minutes, metros, taxis, hospitals close by. The price is jams, noise, dirty air and danger in crossing the road.

perspectives.who: Village residents and rural researchers
perspectives.explanation: Village roads are quieter and the air is cleaner. But a sick person may wait hours for a vehicle, and a girl may leave school because it is too far to walk. India's rural roads programme, begun in 2000, was started for this reason.

explanations.art: A picture split down the middle: on one side a crowded city crossing with signals, a flyover and a metro, on the other a village road with a tractor, a bullock cart, cyclists and a goat crossing.
explanations.context: This card delivers the board point of comparing traffic in cities and villages, without treating either as the better place.

explanations.concept: Why jams happen, and why building wider roads often brings them back
explanations.definition: A traffic jam forms when more vehicles try to use a road than it can carry. A jam can also start with no obstacle at all, when one driver brakes and the drivers behind brake harder.
explanations.description: A road is like a pipe. Only so much can flow through. When too many vehicles enter, they slow and stop. But jams also appear from nothing. In 2008 Yuki Sugiyama and his team in Japan put 22 cars on a circular track and asked the drivers to keep a steady speed. Within minutes one driver slowed a little. The one behind slowed more. Soon a clump of stopped cars was creeping backwards round the circle. What about building a wider road? Studies of many cities found that new road space fills up within a few years. Easier driving brings out more drivers.
examples: A jam on a highway often has no accident at its front. It is a wave of braking passing backwards down the line.
After a new flyover opens, traffic moves well for a year or two and then thickens again.
Ants on a busy trail hardly ever jam. In tests reported in 2019, Argentine ants kept moving smoothly even when their bridge was four-fifths full.

perspectives.who: Gilles Duranton and Matthew Turner, economists, in a study of American cities in 2011
perspectives.explanation: Driving rises in step with road building, almost one for one. Building roads to cure jams does not work. Charging for road use at busy hours and running good public transport do.

perspectives.who: Road engineers and many city governments
perspectives.explanation: A growing city does need more roads and bridges, and a new road lets more people travel even if it is full. The jam returns, but more journeys are being made.

perspectives.who: Audrey Dussutour and colleagues, who study ants, in 2019
perspectives.explanation: Ants avoid jams because each ant adjusts to the others. When the trail is crowded they slow slightly, and they stop joining the trail when it is too full. No ant tries to get ahead of the rest.

explanations.art: A circular track seen from above with 22 small cars, most evenly spaced and a tight clump of five on one side with a backward arrow, and beside it a twig bridge with ants crossing in tidy lanes.
explanations.context: This card explains a city jam with a real experiment, and compares it with how ants manage a crowded path.

explanations.concept: Bullocks, horses and camels who pull carts are workers who tire, feel heat and need rest
explanations.definition: A draught animal is an animal who pulls or carries loads for people. Indian law limits how long and in what heat such animals may be worked.
explanations.description: A tractor can be left in the sun all day. A bullock cannot. Animals who pull carts are living beings who do a job. They get tired and thirsty. They feel the heat, the weight and the whip. India has a law for them. Rules made in 1965 say a working animal must not be worked for more than nine hours in a day. In the hottest part of a hot day, the animal must rest. An animal who is sick, hurt or too young must not be worked at all. A good cart owner knows each animal's ways and looks after them like a partner.
examples: At Pongal in Tamil Nadu, on the day called Mattu Pongal, cattle are bathed, their horns are painted and they are fed sweet rice.
A bullock cart with rubber tyres and good bearings is far easier to pull than one with wooden wheels.
Hand-pulled rickshaws, in which a person does this work for other people, still run in parts of Kolkata.

perspectives.who: Farmers and cart owners
perspectives.explanation: A bullock eats straw from the farm, gives dung for the field and goes where no lorry can. For a small farmer the animal is both family and livelihood.

perspectives.who: Animal rights thinkers such as Peter Singer, in 'Animal Liberation', 1975
perspectives.explanation: An animal cannot agree to work and cannot leave. Using another being as an engine is wrong however kindly it is done, now that machines can do the job.

perspectives.who: N. S. Ramaswamy, an Indian management teacher who studied animal power from the 1970s
perspectives.explanation: He counted crores of working animals in India and argued for better carts, harnesses and animal health care. In his view the animals did a large share of the country's haulage and were being ignored.

explanations.art: Two bullocks resting in the shade of a neem tree at noon, yoke lifted off, drinking from a trough while the cart stands beside them.
explanations.context: This card treats working animals as beings with needs, and gives the law that protects them.

explanations.concept: Living travellers carry their own fuel: a small bird can fly for eleven days without landing
explanations.definition: Migrating animals store energy from food as body fat before a long journey and use it up as they travel.
explanations.description: People are not the only ones who make long journeys. A bird called the bar-tailed godwit flies from Alaska to New Zealand and Australia every year. In 2022 a young godwit wearing a tiny tracker flew about 13,500 kilometres in 11 days without landing once. Before leaving, godwits eat until nearly half their body is fat. That fat is their fuel tank. Amur falcons gather in Nagaland every autumn in lakhs. Then they cross the Arabian Sea to Africa without a rest, more than 3,000 kilometres over water. Their long flights are paid for by the fat they stored, as a bus journey is paid for by the fuel in its tank.
examples: A monarch butterfly crosses North America on the sugar of flower nectar.
A coconut can float across an ocean on the currents and sprout on a far beach, using no fuel at all.
Before the flight, a godwit's stomach and gut shrink to save weight, as a racing cyclist strips a cycle.
explanations.one_view: These journeys were recorded by satellite trackers. They are here so that human vehicles are seen beside the other great travellers of the Earth.
explanations.art: A map of the Pacific Ocean with a dotted line from Alaska to Tasmania and a small long-billed bird flying along the line, and an inset of falcons filling the sky over a lake in Nagaland.
explanations.context: This card shows that other animals also solve the problem of fuel for travel, with their own bodies.

explanations.concept: Wheels and carts are about 5,500 years old, and Harappan children played with toy carts
explanations.definition: The wheel is a round frame that turns on a central rod called an axle. Wheeled carts appear in the records of several regions from about 3500 BCE.
explanations.description: Dragging a load is hard, because the whole underside rubs on the ground. A wheel rolls, so it rubs only at the axle. The oldest signs of wheeled carts are about 5,500 years old. They come from Mesopotamia, from eastern Europe and from the lands north of the Black Sea, at nearly the same time. Nobody knows who was first. In the cities of the Indus valley, at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, people made small clay carts with solid wheels more than 4,000 years ago. Many seem to have been toys. Bullock carts in Sindh and Punjab kept nearly the same shape into modern times.
examples: The stone chariot at Hampi in Karnataka shows how much the wheel meant to its builders. So do the great stone wheels of the Sun temple at Konark in Odisha.
The peoples of ancient Mexico made wheeled toys but used no carts. They had no large animals to pull them and their land was steep.

perspectives.who: Katha Upanishad 1.3.3 and 1.3.4
perspectives.explanation: This old text pictures a person as a chariot, with the body as the vehicle, the senses as the horses and the mind as the reins. Its teachers chose the best vehicle of their day as the picture. The roots page gives the verse in full.

perspectives.who: The Ramayana, in its account of the Pushpaka vimana
perspectives.explanation: The epic describes a flying chariot that went wherever its owner wished. This is a work of imagination, showing that people dreamed of a vehicle with no animals long before one existed. It is not evidence of ancient aircraft.

perspectives.who: Archaeologists such as David Anthony, in 2007
perspectives.explanation: The wheel spread very quickly once it appeared, so its birthplace is hard to pin down. It needed good woodworking tools of metal, and that may be why it appeared when it did.

explanations.art: A small terracotta toy cart with two solid wheels and a pair of clay bullocks, on a brick floor, with a child's hand reaching for it.
explanations.context: This card gives the long history of the wheel in India and elsewhere, and how old texts used the chariot as an idea.

explanations.concept: Who is a road for? Most Indians walk, cycle or take the bus, and most road space goes to cars
explanations.definition: Road space is shared among walkers, cyclists, buses, two-wheelers, cars and goods vehicles. How to divide it is a choice that cities argue about.
explanations.description: Look at a city road and ask who uses it. In the 2011 census, about one in three working Indians who travelled to work went on foot or by cycle. Many more took a bus. Only a few went by car. Now look at how the road is built. Most of the width is for motor vehicles. The footpath is narrow, broken or missing. About 1.7 lakh people died on India's roads in 2022, and about one in five were walking. So people ask a fair question. Should a city be built so that cars move fast, or so that people can get about safely?
examples: Chennai adopted a policy in 2014 that put walking and cycling first, and rebuilt many footpaths wide enough for a wheelchair.
Count the footpath on your own street. Is it wide enough for two people to pass? Is there a slope at the kerb?
On 'Raahgiri' days in Gurugram, Bhopal and other cities, a road is closed to motor vehicles for a morning. People walk, skate and play on it.

perspectives.who: Enrique Peñalosa, mayor of Bogotá in Colombia from 1998
perspectives.explanation: A good city is one where a child on a tricycle can go anywhere safely. He took road space from cars for buses, cycle tracks and footpaths. He said a bus with 80 people has a right to 80 times the road space of a car with one.

perspectives.who: Jane Jacobs, a writer in New York, in 1961
perspectives.explanation: Streets are where a city's life happens: shops, children, neighbours watching out for each other. She led residents in stopping a highway that planners wanted to drive through their neighbourhood.

perspectives.who: Planners who favour fast roads, and many vehicle owners
perspectives.explanation: Goods, ambulances and workers must move quickly for a city to earn its living. People who have saved for years to buy a vehicle want roads they can use.

explanations.art: A street seen from above divided into coloured strips for walkers, cyclists, a bus lane and cars, with small figures showing how many people each strip carries.
explanations.context: This card turns the fuel question into a question about fairness on the road.

agreed.text: The amount of carbon dioxide in the air has risen by about half since people began burning fossil fuels in large amounts.
agreed.evidence: Charles David Keeling began measuring the air on Mauna Loa, a mountain in Hawaii, in 1958. He found 315 parts of carbon dioxide in every million parts of air. The same station now records more than 420. Air bubbles trapped in old ice show close to 280 before the age of engines.

agreed.text: Lead was once added to petrol, harmed children's brains, and has now been removed everywhere.
agreed.evidence: The geochemist Clair Patterson showed in the 1960s that lead in the air and in people's bodies had risen enormously since leaded petrol began. India stopped selling leaded petrol in 2000. The last country to stop was Algeria, in 2021. Lead in children's blood fell wherever it was removed.

agreed.text: Heavier vehicles need more energy to go the same distance, whatever they run on.
agreed.evidence: Tests of petrol, diesel and electric vehicles all show that energy use climbs with weight. A heavy vehicle rubs harder on the road and needs a bigger push to speed up. This is why a scooter uses a fraction of what a car does.

agreed.text: A helmet and a seat belt greatly reduce the chance of dying in a crash.
agreed.evidence: Reviews of many crash studies agree on this. A proper helmet cuts a two-wheeler rider's risk of death by about two-fifths. A seat belt cuts a front-seat passenger's risk by about half.

challenging.claim: Petroleum did not come from living beings. It formed from carbon deep inside the Earth and is still seeping upward.
challenging.who: Dmitri Mendeleev in 1877, Nikolai Kudryavtsev and other Soviet geologists from 1951, and the astronomer Thomas Gold in the 1980s and 1990s
challenging.for: Simple gases such as methane are found on planets and moons with no known life. Oil sometimes turns up in rocks that never lay under a sea.
challenging.against: Oil contains molecules that are plainly the worn remains of molecules from living cells. A deep hole drilled in Sweden from 1986 to test Gold's idea found only traces of oil, far too little to matter. Oil companies find oil by looking where ancient life was buried, and it works.
challenging.context: Almost everyone says oil came from ancient life. A few well-known scientists said it did not. Their idea was tested and failed, and it shows that even a firm textbook fact has been challenged.

challenging.claim: Hydrogen, and not batteries, will power the vehicles of the future.
challenging.who: Car makers such as Toyota and Hyundai, and India's National Green Hydrogen Mission of 2023
challenging.for: Hydrogen is a gas that gives only water when used in a device called a fuel cell. A tank fills in minutes and carries a lorry a long way without a heavy battery.
challenging.against: Making hydrogen cleanly needs a great deal of electricity, and much is lost on the way. Charging a battery directly is about three times less wasteful. Few filling stations exist. Many engineers expect hydrogen to be used for ships and steel making and not for cars.
challenging.context: Most people now assume the future is battery vehicles. Some companies and governments are betting on hydrogen. Nobody yet knows who is right, especially for lorries and buses.

challenging.claim: The answer to fuel and traffic problems is fewer vehicles, and not cleaner ones.
challenging.who: Ivan Illich in 'Energy and Equity', 1974, and many city planners today
challenging.for: Illich counted the hours people work to pay for a car, its fuel and its roads. He found that the car then moves them at about the pace of a cyclist. Cities built for walking and cycling use a fraction of the fuel.
challenging.against: Vehicles brought villages within reach of hospitals, schools and markets. People in poorer countries are only now getting what richer ones have long had, and it is unfair to ask them to go without.
challenging.context: Nearly every plan for the future keeps the vehicles and changes what powers them. A minority says the vehicle itself is the problem. It is here so that the child sees that the question can be asked.

challenging.who: A popular belief after the Supreme Court's orders took effect in 2002
challenging.for: Black smoke from buses and autos disappeared, and measurements in the first years showed less soot.
challenging.against: By the 2010s Delhi's air was among the worst in the world again, because of many more vehicles, lorries, dust, industry and burning. Some studies also found that CNG engines give out very fine particles of their own.
challenging.context: The switch to CNG is told as a success story, and in part it was. The later measurements show that one change of fuel does not settle the matter.

big_questions.q: Petrol is sunlight that was caught millions of years ago. Your breakfast is sunlight that was caught a few months ago. So is there any vehicle, or any living traveller, that does not run on the Sun?
big_questions.hint: Try a sailing boat, an electric train and a bird. Follow each one's energy backwards as far as you can.

big_questions.q: You ride a cycle to the shop. What moved the cycle: your legs, your breakfast, the rice plant or the Sun?
big_questions.hint: Ask if you can leave any one of them out and still get to the shop.

big_questions.q: The oil took millions of years to form, and people may burn most of it in a few hundred. Does the oil belong only to the people alive now?
big_questions.hint: Think about children who will be born a hundred years from now, and the beings who became the oil.

big_questions.q: An electric scooter makes no smoke in your street, but a power station far away burns coal to charge it. Is the scooter clean?
big_questions.hint: Ask who breathes the smoke in each case. Does it matter whether you can see them?

big_questions.q: If engines that waste less lead people to drive more, what would actually make a country burn less fuel?
big_questions.hint: Think about what makes your own family decide to make a trip or not.

big_questions.q: A bullock who pulls a cart gets tired and thirsty. A tractor does not seem to. Is it fair to ask an animal to do the work of an engine?
big_questions.hint: Think of what the bullock gets and gives, and of what the bullock would choose if asked.

big_questions.q: Ants on a crowded trail do not jam, and people in cars do. What do the ants do that we do not?
big_questions.hint: Watch a line of ants for five minutes. Look for overtaking, pushing and waiting.

big_questions.q: A village has clean air and few buses. A city has many buses and dirty air. Which would you choose to live in, and what would you change about each?
big_questions.hint: Think about a day when someone in the family is ill, and a day when everyone is well.

big_questions.q: Most people on a road are walking, cycling or in a bus, yet most of the road is given to cars. Who should decide how a road is shared?
big_questions.hint: Imagine you are dividing a road with chalk. Whom would you ask first?

big_questions.q: Scientists can measure energy exactly, in a litre of petrol or a plate of idlis, but cannot say what energy is. Can you really know something that you can only measure?
big_questions.hint: Think of something else you can count or measure without being able to say what it is, such as time.

story.title: How Old Is Your Sunlight?
story.note: A made-up story set in Chennai and in a village near Pollachi, Tamil Nadu. The family and the bullock are imagined. What is real: petroleum formed from tiny sea beings over millions of years, the energy in food and in fossil fuel was first caught from sunlight, and coconut farms around Pollachi use bullock carts, tractors and lorries side by side.
text: Kuzhali lived in Chennai, and she knew about traffic. Her school was six kilometres from her flat. On a good day the car took thirty minutes. On a bad day it took an hour, and she ate her idlis in the back seat looking at the same bus advertisement the whole time.
In the Pongal holidays she went to stay with her cousin Sevanthi, in a village near Pollachi. Sevanthi was eight, a year older, and she knew about everything else.

On the first morning Sevanthi wheeled out two cycles. 'School is closed, but I will show you my road,' she said. They rode three kilometres between coconut trees. It took fifteen minutes. In all that way they met one bus, four motorcycles, a tractor, eleven goats and a peacock who would not move.
'Where is everybody?' asked Kuzhali.
'This is everybody,' said Sevanthi.

At the farm, their aunt Ponni was under the tractor with a spanner. Ponni athai mended every engine for ten villages around. Beside the shed stood a cart heaped with coconuts, and in front of the cart stood a bullock named Karuppan, chewing slowly, the colour of a monsoon cloud.
'Athai,' said Kuzhali, 'which is the best vehicle? I am making a list.' She had a notebook. 'The car is the fastest. So the car is first.'
'Is it?' said Sevanthi. 'You said six kilometres takes you an hour. I can cycle six kilometres in half an hour. My cycle beats your car.'
'Only in Chennai,' said Kuzhali, and then she heard what she had said.
'The tractor is the strongest,' said Ponni athai from underneath. 'It pulls what twenty people could not. So is the tractor first?'
'Karuppan is the quietest,' said Sevanthi. 'He needs no road. He goes between the trees where the tractor cannot turn. He finds his own way home if you fall asleep on the cart.'
'A car cannot do that,' Kuzhali agreed. She looked at her list. It had three firsts on it now. 'Then I will ask it another way. Which one eats the least?'
Ponni athai slid out and sat up, wiping her hands. 'Now that is a mechanic's question. What does Karuppan eat?'
'Grass. Straw. Oilcake.'
'And what did the grass eat?'
Kuzhali knew this from school. 'Sunlight. And water and air.'
'When?'
'When? This year, I suppose. After the rains.'
'Good. Karuppan runs on this season's sunlight. What do you run on, when you pedal?'
'Idli,' said Kuzhali. 'Rice. The rice grew... last year?'
'Last year's sunlight. Now.' Ponni athai tapped the tractor's tank, and it rang. 'Diesel. Where from?'
'From under the ground.'

'And before that, tiny beings in an old sea, smaller than a grain of dust. They lived on sunlight as grass does. They died and sank and were buried, and the Earth cooked them slowly into oil. How long ago?'
Kuzhali did not know.

'Before there were people. Before there were coconut trees. Crores of years.' Ponni athai looked at the tractor almost kindly. 'So this fellow runs on the oldest sunlight of all. Sunlight that fell before anyone had eyes to see it.'

Kuzhali looked at the bullock, the cycle and the tractor. A minute ago they had been three different kinds of thing. 'They are all eating the Sun,' she said. 'Only the age is different. This year's, last year's, and crores of years old.'
'Then here is the question for your notebook,' said Ponni athai. 'Grass grows back by next rains. Rice grows back by next harvest. How long before the old sea makes more diesel?'
Kuzhali did the sum and did not like it. 'Crores of years.'
'And when we burn it, where does it go?'
Sevanthi answered. 'Into the air. Teacher said it makes the air hold more heat.'
'So you two tell me,' said Ponni athai. 'Which sunlight should we spend first? The kind that comes back every year, or the kind that came once?'
Nobody spoke. Karuppan swished his tail.
'But Athai,' said Kuzhali at last, 'you mend diesel engines. That is your work.'

'It is,' said Ponni athai. 'Without this tractor, the coconuts do not reach the lorry and the lorry does not reach Chennai, and you do not get chutney with your idli. I did not say the answer was easy. I said it was your question.' She picked up her spanner. 'Last month I put a solar panel on the pump shed. That is today's sunlight, not even one day old. I am an old mechanic learning a new engine.'

That evening Kuzhali crossed out her list. On a clean page she wrote three words in a column: today, this year, long ago. Then she sat on the cart beside Karuppan, who smelt of hay, and tried to work out which column she belonged in herself.
story.epiphany: A bullock, a cyclist and a tractor all run on energy that was first caught from the Sun. What differs is how long ago it was caught, and so how soon it can be had again.
ask: Kuzhali's list had three 'firsts'. Is there one best vehicle, or does it depend on what you ask?
Which sunlight would you spend first: this year's or the kind that came once? What makes that hard to do?
Kuzhali tried to work out which column she belonged in. Which would you put yourself in?
art: Two girls on cycles on a narrow road between coconut trees, stopped by a peacock standing in the middle.
A woman mechanic sitting on the ground beside a red tractor, spanner in hand, with a grey bullock and a cart of coconuts behind her and two girls listening.
A notebook page with three words in a column, 'today', 'this year', 'long ago', and small drawings beside them of a solar panel, a bullock and a tractor.

how_we_found_out.story: For most of the time that people have burned coal and oil, they believed that smoke simply blows away. The sky is so large that nothing people did could change it. That was reasonable. A chimney's smoke thins out and is gone within minutes. In 1856 Eunice Foote, an American scientist, tested gases in glass tubes set in sunlight, with a thermometer in each. The tube filled with carbon dioxide grew much hotter than the tube of ordinary air and took far longer to cool. She wrote that more of this gas in the air would make the Earth warmer. As a woman, she did not present her paper at the science meeting that year. A male scientist, Joseph Henry, read it out for her, and it was soon forgotten. In 1859 John Tyndall in London made finer measurements and is usually given the credit. In 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated the warming by hand. Still nobody knew if the gas was really building up. In 1958 Charles David Keeling began measuring the air on a mountain in Hawaii, far from any city. His record climbed year after year, and has not stopped. Foote's paper was found again in 2011 by a retired geologist, Raymond Sorenson.
how_we_found_out.who: Eunice Foote, Joseph Henry, John Tyndall, Svante Arrhenius, Charles David Keeling, Raymond Sorenson
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed that smoke from burning fuel blows away and cannot change something as vast as the air. It was believable because smoke does thin out and vanish from sight within minutes.

roots.context: You have followed the push in a cycle, a bullock cart and a bus back to where it came from. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A pump fills a scooter's tank with petrol in one minute. That petrol took millions of years to make, from tiny sea beings who lived and died long before any person. So a ride on a petrol scooter is paid for by beings from the far past, and spent in minutes. A ride on a cycle is paid for by this year's rice, which grows again. The two rides differ in how old the push is and in how fast it is used up.
deep_truth.habit: We think of fuel as something that begins at the pump, bought and used on the same day. The pump hides the long road behind the fuel: the sea beings, the millions of years, the mud, the heat and the drilling.
deep_truth.evidence: A bus burns a litre of diesel in a few minutes of driving. That litre took millions of years to form. People began burning oil in large amounts only a century and a half ago, and the world now burns about 10 crore barrels a day. Rice, grass and sugarcane grow back in a year, and the old sea cannot do that.

three.who_am_i: You are fed by this year's harvest, and you travel on a road that is also fed by beings who died before there were people. Whenever you ride in a petrol vehicle, you are spending something that was left behind for no one in particular.
three.what_is_life: Life does not only use energy while it lives. When the tiny sea beings died, the sunlight stored in their bodies stayed in the rock for millions of years. A death can become a store for someone else's journey.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth stores slowly and people spend quickly. Each time you walk, share a ride or burn less, you decide how fast to spend what the Earth took millions of years to make.

roots.thread: Ask of anything that moves, 'what is pushing it?', and keep asking. Almost every answer on a road leads back to the Sun, through a leaf or a tiny sea being. What changes from one answer to the next is the age of the push and how fast we use it up. How we spend that store is then a question about everyone, including beings long dead and children not yet born. The old Indian teachers used the chariot as their picture of a person, and asked who is really riding. A Buddhist teacher answered that there is no rider to be found, and his view is given below.

teachings.teaching: Know the self as the rider and the body as the chariot. Know the understanding as the driver and the mind as the reins. The senses, they say, are the horses, and the things they sense are the roads.
teachings.link: The lesson asked what moves a vehicle and followed the answer back through engine, fuel and Sun. The Upanishad asks the same question of a person: when the body moves, who or what is moving it? Science can trace the energy. It has not found the rider.

teachings.teaching: Seven yoke the chariot that has one wheel. One horse with seven names draws it. The wheel has three hubs, does not wear out and cannot be stopped, and on it all these worlds rest.
teachings.link: The poets pictured the Sun as a single chariot on which all worlds depend. The lesson's science agrees with the plain part: the movement of nearly every living body and every engine on Earth is drawn from the Sun.

teachings.teaching: The Sun is to be honoured as Brahman, the ground of all. When the Sun was born, the text says, shouts of joy arose, and all beings and all that they desire rose up with it.
teachings.link: The text ties every being and every wish to the Sun's rising. In terms of energy, a scientist can say much the same: the food, the wind, the rain and the fuel all rise with the Sun.

science.text: The energy in food, wood, wind, flowing rivers and fossil fuels all came first from sunlight. The energy of the Earth's inner heat, of the tides and of nuclear power did not.
Energy is never made or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. What energy is in itself has no agreed answer.

other_view.who: The Buddhist monk Nagasena, in the Milindapanha, book 2, chapter 1
other_view.view: Nagasena asks King Milinda how he came, and the king says by chariot. 'Is the pole the chariot? The axle? The wheels? The frame?' To each the king says no. 'Then where is the chariot?' Nagasena's point is that 'chariot' is only a name for parts that have come together, and a person is the same. On this view there is no rider behind the body and no one ground behind the many forms. There are only parts and causes, flowing on.

practice.title: Follow it back
practice.say: Sit by a window where you can see the road or hear it. Pick one thing that is moving: a scooter, a bird, a person walking. Now follow it back, slowly, out loud. What is pushing it? Where did that come from? And before that? Keep going until you reach the Sun or get stuck. Now put a hand on your chest and feel your own breathing. Follow that back too. Sit for three slow breaths.
practice.kid: Look out of a window. Pick one moving thing. Ask: what is pushing it? Where did that come from? Keep asking until you reach the Sun. Then do the same for your own breath.

ask: If the bus and you both run on sunlight, what is the real difference between a machine moving and a living being moving?
The tiny sea beings who became oil lived and died long before people. Are they part of your bus ride?
When you follow a push all the way back, does it ever reach a place where it truly starts?

open_questions.q: What will most vehicles run on fifty years from now?
open_questions.why_open: Batteries are ahead for scooters and cars. Hydrogen, plant fuels and new kinds of battery are all being tried for lorries, ships and aeroplanes. Which wins depends on discoveries and prices that nobody can predict.

open_questions.q: Can a battery be made without scarce metals and without harming the people who mine them?
open_questions.why_open: Batteries using sodium, which comes from common salt, have begun to be sold. They hold less energy for their weight. Whether they can replace lithium and cobalt widely is not yet known.
Physicists can calculate energy and have found that the total never changes. The physicist Richard Feynman wrote that physics has no knowledge of what energy is. It remains a number that works.

open_questions.q: How much oil is left, and will it run out before people stop wanting it?
open_questions.why_open: Estimates of oil in the ground keep changing as new methods reach more of it. Whether demand will fall first, because of cleaner vehicles and climate rules, is argued among geologists and economists.

open_questions.q: How do ants keep their trails flowing without anyone in charge, and can human traffic copy them?
open_questions.why_open: Experiments show that ants adjust their speed and stop entering a crowded trail. The exact rules each ant follows are still being worked out, and human drivers do not behave like ants.

open_questions.q: Who first made a wheel, and where?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest evidence appears in several regions within a few hundred years of about 3500 BCE. Wood rots, so the first wheels are almost certainly lost, and the dates are too close to tell apart.

experiments.title: Balloon rocket: does more air carry it farther?
experiments.context: A balloon rocket shows how a stored push turns into movement. You try three amounts of air and see how far each one carries the balloon along a string.
experiments.question: If you blow twice as much air into a balloon, does it travel twice as far along the string?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will double the air carry the balloon double the distance, a little farther, or the same? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the number of breaths: 2, 4 and 6. Keep the same balloon, the same straw, the same string, the same person blowing and the same start mark. Try each amount 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a smooth thread or nylon string, about 4 metres long (wool and rough twine will not work)
a drinking straw, plastic or paper
long balloons, one to use and two spare
sticky tape, two strips stuck ready to the edge of a table
two chairs, or a window bar and a door handle
a school ruler of 30 centimetres, or a measuring tape
sticky notes or small paper squares to mark where the balloon stops
pencil and paper for the results table

experiments.safety: A burst balloon leaves small pieces that a child under 5 can choke on, so pick up every piece at once. Tie the string at about chair-back height, never at face height.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Write each distance in ruler lengths (one school ruler is 30 centimetres). Circle the middle value for each amount of air. If the balloon reaches the far end, write END.

setup.art: A drinking straw threaded on a long smooth string stretched between two chair backs in a living room.
setup.caption: 1. Thread the straw on the string and pull the string tight between two chairs.

setup.art: A long balloon with its neck pinched, taped under the straw with the balloon body pointing along the string.
setup.caption: 2. Blow the balloon, pinch the neck, and tape it under the straw.

setup.art: A sticky note on the string at the point where the balloon stopped, with a ruler laid beside the string.
setup.caption: 3. After the balloon stops, mark the place and measure from the start.

setup.art: A results table with three rows labelled 2, 4 and 6 breaths, with a pencil beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Write each distance in the table, three tries for each amount of air.

flow.do: Take about 4 metres of smooth thread. Push one end through a straw. Tie the two ends tight to two chair backs, so the string is straight and level. Stick a sticky note on the string near one chair for the start mark.
flow.say: We are making a track for a balloon rocket. The string must be tight and straight, or the balloon will wobble.
flow.kid: Thread the straw on the string. Help to tie it tight between two chairs.
flow.parent: Use smooth thread or nylon fishing line. Wool and rough twine slow the straw too much. The string should be at chair-back height. If the string sags, pull the chairs further apart.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess. Write the guess in the margin of the table before any test. Then ask for the reason.
flow.say: We will try 2, 4 and 6 breaths. Will double the air carry the balloon double the distance? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what will happen if you put in more air. Say why you think so.

ask.q: What do you think more air will do to the distance, and why?
good: More air gives a bigger push, so it goes farther.
Any honest guess with a reason, such as 'the same, because it is the same balloon'.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A guess is a guess, and the test will answer it.

flow.do: Blow up a balloon with 2 big breaths of your own. Pinch the neck so that no air escapes. Your child tapes the balloon under the straw, with the neck pointing back to the start mark. Pull the straw to the start. Count 3, 2, 1, then let go. Mark where the balloon stops with a sticky note.
flow.say: Count with me. Three, two, one, go! Watch where the balloon stops.
flow.kid: Count 3, 2, 1. Let go. Mark where it stops.

ask.q: Where do you think the air goes when you let go?
good: Out of the neck, backwards.
It pushes backwards, and the balloon goes forwards.

flow.parent: Each try needs a fresh breath of air. Blow out the old air and tape the balloon again. Do this 3 times for 2 breaths. A big breath means breathing all the way out. If the balloon pops, use a spare one and repeat that try. A balloon grows softer with use, so tell your child that the first tries may go a little shorter.

flow.do: Do the same with 4 big breaths, three times. Measure each try from the start mark to the sticky note, using the ruler end to end. Write the number of ruler lengths in the table.
flow.say: This time we use 4 breaths. Count the ruler lengths each time. Which try went farthest?
flow.kid: Do three tries with 4 breaths. Count ruler lengths. Write them in the table.
flow.parent: Lay the ruler end to end along the string and count. If you have a measuring tape, use it, and write centimetres in the table in place of ruler lengths. Keep the same unit all through.

flow.do: Do the same with 6 breaths, three times. If the balloon reaches the end of the string, write END in the table.
flow.say: Now 6 breaths. Is it going farther than before? Is it going twice as far as 2 breaths?
flow.kid: Do three tries with 6 breaths. Write each distance in the table.
flow.parent: If your string is short and the balloon reaches the end each time, that already shows that more air carries it farther. For a longer run, move the chairs apart.

flow.do: Circle the middle value of each amount of air. Compare with the guess you made. Ask what the test cannot tell us.
flow.say: Look at your circled numbers. Did double the air give double the distance? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Circle the middle number for each amount. Was your guess right?

ask.q: Did double the air give double the distance? Where do you think the rest of the push went?
good: More air always went farther, but not exactly double.
Some push is lost to rubbing on the straw and to pushing the air aside.

ask.q: What could we test next?
good: A longer string, a different balloon, or a bigger balloon.
Weight on the balloon, which is the next experiment.

flow.parent: The result is usually that more air goes farther, but double the air does not give double the distance. A part of the push is lost to rubbing between the straw and the string and to pushing the air in front of the balloon aside. The test cannot say exactly how much air is in each balloon. Breaths differ in size, so the amounts are only roughly 2, 4 and 6. Scientists measure air with a bag of known size. The idea to leave your child with is that the push was stored in the balloon and came out as movement.
flow.think: If the balloon holds a push, where did you get that push from?

experiments.title: A load on the rocket: does a heavy balloon go as far?
experiments.context: This test uses the same balloon rocket and string. You add coins as a load and see if the balloon still goes as far, which shows why heavy vehicles need more push.
experiments.question: If the balloon rocket carries coins, does it go as far with the same amount of air?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will 2 coins and then 4 coins make the balloon go a little less far, a lot less far, or the same? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the number of coins: 0, 2 and 4. Use 4 breaths of air every time, with the same balloon, straw, string and start mark. Try each load 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: the balloon rocket string, straw, balloon and tape from the first test
4 one-rupee coins
a school ruler of 30 centimetres, or a measuring tape
sticky notes to mark where the balloon stops
two spare balloons

experiments.safety: A burst balloon leaves small pieces that a child under 5 can choke on, so pick up every piece at once.
experiments.record: Fill in the table with ruler lengths. Circle the middle value for each load.
