flow.say: Last time more air went farther. Now we add coins to the balloon but keep the air the same. What do you think will happen? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what coins will do. Say why you think so.

ask.q: Will the balloon go as far when it carries coins?
good: No, it is heavier, so the same push moves it less far.
Any honest guess with a reason.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess.

flow.do: Do 3 tries with no coins and 4 breaths. Mark and measure each one. Write the ruler lengths down.
flow.say: First the plain balloon, with no coins. This is the one to compare with.
flow.kid: Do three tries with no coins. Write the distances.
flow.parent: If you did the 4 breath test in the first experiment, you can use those numbers. Repeat one try to check that today's balloon behaves the same.

flow.do: Tape 2 coins in a row along the balloon's belly, close to the straw. Do 3 tries with 4 breaths. Mark and measure each one.
flow.say: Now 2 coins. The air is the same. Watch the balloon. Is it as fast as before?
flow.kid: Tape 2 coins on. Do three tries. Write the distances.
flow.parent: Keep the balloon level. Coins hanging at one end tilt the balloon and slow it. If the tape slips, press it down firmly with your thumb.

flow.do: Do the same with 4 coins. If the balloon barely moves, write 0 for that try. Then try 2 coins again.
flow.say: Now 4 coins. Does it go as far as with 2? What is happening to the same push?
flow.kid: Tape 4 coins on. Do three tries. Write the distances.

ask.q: Why does a heavier balloon go less far with the same air?
good: The same push has more weight to move.
It takes more push to move something heavy.

flow.parent: If four coins stop the balloon, that is a result, not a failure. It shows that this much air cannot move that much weight.

activities.title: What will make the toy car go?
activities.context: This is the first look at the big question. A toy car sits still, and you find every way to make it move and say what pushed it each time.

materials.item: a toy car, or a small box, a steel katori or a chappal to use in its place
a clear floor, about 2 metres of it
a hardback book to make a slope

schedule.what: Find ways to make the car move and say what pushed it each time.

activities.record: Draw the toy car and one arrow for each way you made it move. Write what gave the push next to each arrow.

setup.art: A toy car sitting still on a clean floor with nothing near it.
setup.caption: 1. Put the car on the floor and look at it. Does it move?

setup.art: Four small pictures: a hand pushing the car, a string pulling the car, a tilted book with the car on it, a puff of breath blowing the car.
setup.caption: 2. Find as many ways as you can to make it move.

flow.do: Put the toy car on the floor. Ask your child to look at it for 20 seconds without touching it. Then ask what it is doing.
flow.say: Look at the car. Is it going anywhere? Why not?
flow.kid: Look at the car. Does it move by itself?

ask.q: Will the car ever move by itself?
good: No. Something has to push it or pull it.
Not unless the floor tilts or someone touches it.

flow.do: Ask your child to find as many ways as possible to make the car move. Use a push with a finger, a puff of breath, a string pulling it and a slope made from a book. Say aloud what gave the push each time.
flow.say: Find different ways to make the car go. Each time, tell me what gave the push.
flow.kid: Make the car move in four different ways. Say what pushed it each time.

ask.q: What gave the push each time?
good: A finger, a breath of air, a pull from a string, and gravity on a slope.
Anything that pushes or pulls, from your own body or from the Earth.

flow.parent: A real vehicle cannot be pushed by hand. The question for the rest of the lesson is what pushes it, and where the push comes from.

flow.do: Draw the car and four arrows on paper. Write what gave the push next to each arrow.
flow.say: Draw the car. Draw one arrow for each push. Write what gave the push.
flow.kid: Draw the car and four arrows. Write what pushed it.
flow.think: Where did the push in your finger come from?

activities.title: Five-minute traffic count from a window or a gate
activities.context: In this activity you count what goes past in five minutes and sort it. You then compare your tally with a tally from a place of a different kind, such as a relative's village or a city.

materials.item: a window, a balcony or a gate that looks onto a road, and a grown-up with you
a clipboard or a hard book with paper and a pencil
a phone or a watch that can time 5 minutes

schedule.what: Make the tally sheet, count for five minutes, add up and compare.

activities.record: A tally sheet with rows for: walkers, cycles, two-wheelers, autos, cars, buses, lorries, animal carts and others. Put a mark in the row each time one goes past. Count marks in fives.
activities.safety: Count from a window, a balcony or a gate, with a grown-up beside you. Never stand on the road.

setup.art: A paper divided into nine rows with a vehicle sketch in each row: walker, cycle, two-wheeler, auto, car, bus, lorry, animal cart, other.
setup.caption: 1. Draw nine rows on a sheet of paper and name each row.

setup.art: A child at a window with a clipboard making tally marks while a parent holds a phone timer.
setup.caption: 2. Watch the road for five minutes and make a mark for each one.

setup.art: A tally sheet with marks in groups of five and a total at the bottom of each row.
setup.caption: 3. Add up each row and find the biggest and the smallest.

flow.do: Draw the tally sheet with nine rows. Name each row. Show your child how to make a mark and how to cross four marks with a fifth.
flow.say: We will count what goes past in five minutes. We will make one mark each time, and cross four marks with a fifth.
flow.kid: Draw nine rows. Name each one. Learn to make groups of five marks.
flow.parent: If you live in a very quiet place, count for ten minutes. A busy road may need two counters, one for each direction.

flow.do: Sit at the window or gate with your child. Start the timer for 5 minutes. Both of you watch the road. Make a mark for each one that goes past. Say which kind to your child whenever they are not sure.
flow.say: Ready, steady, count! Make a mark in the right row for each one that passes.
flow.kid: Watch the road. Make a mark for each one that goes past.

ask.q: Before you add up, which row do you think will have the most marks?
good: Any guess with a reason, such as 'scooters, because I see many'.
The kind they see most often near their home.

flow.parent: Walkers count too. A grown-up counts what the child misses, and the numbers need not be exact.

flow.do: Add up each row. Ask your child to find the row with most marks and the row with the fewest. Ask how many vehicles with engines there were in all, leaving out walkers and cycles.
flow.say: Which row has the most? Which has the fewest? How many went past with an engine?
flow.kid: Add up each row. Find the biggest and the smallest.

ask.q: Which kind of traffic was the most, and was it what you expected?
good: Answers will differ. For example, 'two-wheelers' in a city street.
Whatever the tally shows, compared with the guess.

flow.do: Ask a relative or a friend in a different kind of place, a city or a village, to count for 5 minutes. They tell you the numbers on a call. Write them in a second column. Then compare the two columns.
flow.say: Let us ask someone in a different kind of place to count. Then we can see what is the same and what is different.
flow.kid: Call someone who lives in a different kind of place. Compare your tallies.

ask.q: How are the two tallies different, and why?
good: A city has more vehicles and many kinds of engines. A village has more cycles, walkers and animal carts.
People in a village have fewer vehicles and the roads are quieter.

flow.parent: If no one is free to count, count at two different times of day instead, such as morning and evening. Then compare those two tallies.

activities.title: Wind in a sail: a paper boat that moves by breath
activities.context: People sailed for thousands of years with no fuel at all. In this activity you make a boat with a sail and find out how to catch moving air.

materials.item: a wide steel tray, a plastic tub or a big basin, with about 3 centimetres of water
a boat made from a piece of thick paper, a flat cork, a plastic bottle cap or a small plastic lid
paper squares of different sizes, about 5 and 10 centimetres, for sails
a toothpick, a straw piece or a pencil to hold the sail up, with a lump of clay or sticky tape
a drinking straw to blow through
a towel to wipe up spills

schedule.what: Build the boat, test without a sail, then with a small sail and a big sail.

activities.record: Draw the three tests: no sail, small sail, big sail. Write how far the boat moved across the tray each time, in hand-widths.
activities.safety: Pour water carefully and wipe the floor at once. Empty the tray into the sink or onto a plant afterwards.

setup.art: A plastic bottle cap floating in a tray of water with a toothpick mast and a small paper sail.
setup.caption: 1. Make a boat from a bottle cap. Stick a toothpick mast in a bit of clay. Add a paper sail.

setup.art: A child blowing through a straw behind a small boat from the same distance each time.
setup.caption: 2. Blow through a straw from the same distance for the same count each time.

setup.art: Three small boats at three distances across the tray: no sail, small sail, big sail.
setup.caption: 3. Compare how far the boat travels with no sail, a small sail and a big sail.

flow.do: Pour about 3 centimetres of water into the tray. Make a boat from a bottle cap. Press a bit of clay into the cap and stand a toothpick in it as the mast. Make a paper sail for the mast. A grown-up helps with the toothpick.
flow.say: We are building a sailing boat. The sail catches the moving air. Where do you think the push will come from?
flow.kid: Make a boat with a mast. Add a paper sail. Float it in the tray.
flow.parent: The toothpick has a sharp end, so the grown-up handles it. Push it into the clay, with the point down. Any very light floating thing can be the boat.

flow.do: Float the boat with no sail at one end. Blow through a straw from 20 centimetres away, for a count of 3. Mark where the boat stops. Repeat 3 times.
flow.say: First, no sail. Blow for three counts. How far does the boat go?
flow.kid: Blow the plain boat for three counts. See how far it goes.

ask.q: Does the plain boat go far, and what pushes it?
good: It moves a little. Your breath pushes it.
Yes, a little, because the moving air pushes the cap.

flow.parent: Blow from the same distance and for the same count each time, so that the test is fair.

flow.do: Put on the small sail. Blow for 3 counts from the same distance and mark where the boat stops. Repeat 3 times. Then swap to the big sail and repeat 3 times.
flow.say: Now a sail. Blow just the same. Which boat goes farthest, small sail or big sail?
flow.kid: Try the small sail. Then try the big sail. Blow the same each time.

ask.q: Which sail went farthest, and why do you think so?
good: The big sail, because it catches more moving air.
A bigger sail has more cloth for the air to push.

flow.parent: A big sail catches more air, so it usually goes farther. If the boat spins, turn the sail to face the straw and try again. If the tray is too small, use a bigger tub.

flow.do: Look at the three drawings. Ask what pushed the boat and where that air got its push.
flow.say: The wind pushes a real ship the same way. Where do you think a real wind gets its push?
flow.kid: Draw the three tests. Say what pushed the boat.

ask.q: What pushes a real sailing boat, and where does the wind get its push?
good: The moving air in the sail. Sunshine warms the air and makes it move.
The wind. It starts from the Sun warming the Earth unevenly.

flow.parent: Winds are made when the Sun warms land and sea by different amounts. This is a link back to the Sun for the lesson's big question.
flow.think: Which of your boats did the most work, and how do you know?

activities.title: Fill the bus: how much fuel does each person use?
activities.context: Here you play with grains to see how fuel is shared. A full bus burns more fuel than a car, but it carries many more people, so each person uses less.

materials.item: about 60 grains of dal, rice or small beads to be 'people'
four paper strips or plates for the vehicles: a car, a car with 4, a scooter with 2 and a bus
paper and pencil

schedule.what: Load each vehicle with grain people, then work out the distance one litre carries each person.

activities.record: Draw the four vehicles with their people. Write: kilometres on one litre, how many people, and 'kilometres carried for all the people'.

setup.art: Four paper plates labelled car with 1, car with 4, scooter with 2 and bus with 50, each with grains for people.
setup.caption: 1. Put the right number of grains on each paper vehicle.

setup.art: A table with four rows: vehicle, kilometres on one litre, people, and kilometres for all the people.
setup.caption: 2. Fill the table, row by row.

flow.do: Say that one litre of fuel takes a car 15 kilometres, a scooter 45 kilometres and a bus 4 kilometres. Put 1 grain on the first plate for a car with one person. Put 4 grains on the second plate for a car with four people. Put 2 on the third for a scooter. Put 50 on the fourth for the bus.
flow.say: One litre takes a car 15 kilometres, a scooter 45 and a bus only 4. Each grain is a person. Load the plates.
flow.kid: Put one grain for each person on each paper vehicle.
flow.parent: The numbers are rough everyday figures. Real distances depend on the road, the load and the driver. The point is to compare, not to be exact.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which of the four vehicles carries each person farthest on one litre. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Which vehicle gets each person farthest on one litre? What do you think? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which vehicle carries each person farthest on one litre.

ask.q: Which will carry each person farthest on one litre, and why?
good: Any guess with a reason. Many children say the scooter or the car.
The one with the most people and the fewest kilometres per person, if they work it out.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most people guess the scooter or the car, because the bus uses more fuel.

flow.do: Work out the kilometres for all the people. A car with 1 person is 15 times 1, which is 15. A car with 4 people is 4 times 15, which is 60. A scooter with 2 people is 2 times 45, which is 90. The bus is 50 times 4, which is 200. Write each answer in the table.
flow.say: Multiply the people by the kilometres on one litre. This tells us how much travelling one litre does for everyone together.
flow.kid: Multiply the people by the kilometres. Write each answer.

ask.q: Which has the biggest number, and what does it mean?
good: The bus, with 200. One litre of fuel carries the most people the most distance.
The full bus gets more travel out of one litre than the others.

flow.parent: Use a counting line or the grains to count in 15s, 45s and 4s if multiplying is new. The multiplication tables will help.

flow.do: Remove 40 grains from the bus plate, so that 10 people ride the bus. Work out again. Ask what happens when a bus runs nearly empty.
flow.say: Take 40 people off the bus. Now what is the number for the bus?
flow.kid: Take 40 grains off the bus. Work out the number again.

ask.q: What happens to the bus's number when it is nearly empty, and what does that tell us?
good: 10 times 4 is only 40, which is less than the car with 4 people. An empty bus wastes fuel.
A bus is only a good way to travel when many people ride it.

flow.parent: Full buses are good, and empty ones are not. This is why cities try to have many people using buses.

activities.title: The railway gate or signal: how many engines are switched off?
activities.context: In this activity you watch a closed railway gate or a long red signal. You count the engines that stay on and the engines that are switched off. This shows how much fuel is spent standing still.

materials.item: a railway gate, a long red signal or a school gate where vehicles wait, and a grown-up with you
paper and pencil
a watch or phone to time one waiting period

schedule.what: Watch one closed gate or one long red light, count the engines and find out how long it lasts.

activities.record: Two columns: engines running while waiting, and engines switched off. Write the waiting time in minutes next to them.
activities.safety: Watch from the footpath, a safe distance from the road, with a grown-up. Do not cross a railway line.

setup.art: A child and parent on a footpath beside a closed railway gate with a line of vehicles waiting.
setup.caption: 1. Stand safely on the footpath beside the waiting vehicles.

setup.art: A paper with two columns: engines on, engines off, and a tally in each.
setup.caption: 2. Make a mark in the right column for each waiting vehicle.

flow.do: Find a closed railway gate or a red signal that lasts a minute or more. Stand on the footpath with your child, well away from the road. Check that you can see the vehicles that wait.
flow.say: Vehicles wait here for a long time. Let us see how many keep their engines on.
flow.kid: Stand safely on the footpath. Watch the waiting vehicles.
flow.parent: If there is no railway gate nearby, a long red signal or the gate of a school at pick-up time works as well. Never go on the railway line. Start the watch when the gate closes or the signal turns red.

flow.do: Make a mark in the first column for each vehicle with its engine on. Make a mark in the second for each one with it off. A scooter's engine can be heard, and a car's can be heard or felt. Note the waiting time.
flow.say: How can you tell if an engine is on? Make a mark for each one.
flow.kid: Make a mark for each engine, running or off. Note how long it waits.

ask.q: How can you tell if an engine is running, and what is it doing while the vehicle does not move?
good: You can hear it, or see the exhaust. It burns fuel but the vehicle goes nowhere.
It uses fuel and makes carbon dioxide and nothing is moving.

flow.parent: Idling uses about half a litre to one litre of fuel in an hour. A few minutes does not sound like much, but many vehicles waiting for long add up.

flow.do: Add up the marks. Ask how many engines could have been switched off, and how many tens of vehicles waiting in a day might add up.
flow.say: How many engines were running? How many could have been switched off?
flow.kid: Count each column. Which one is bigger?

ask.q: What could drivers do while waiting, and why might they not?
good: Switch the engine off. Some may think restarting uses more fuel, or may fear the engine will not start.
Many drivers keep it on for the fan or the air conditioning.

flow.parent: For a wait of more than about a minute, switching off saves fuel. A modern engine restarts easily.
flow.think: If every driver switched off at every long wait, how much would a city save in a year?

projects.title: Our family's fuel diary for one week
projects.context: In this project your family writes down every trip that uses an engine for one week. You then look for trips that could be walked, cycled, shared or joined, and try one change.

materials.item: a sheet of paper or a notebook page ruled into columns
a pencil
a map app, or a guess at how far the places are from home

schedule.what: Rule the diary page and talk about which trips you think you take.
Add up, mark the trips that could change and choose one change to try.

projects.record: Columns: day, where we went, about how many kilometres, how many people went, and a letter. Write W if the trip could have been walked, C cycled, S shared or J joined with another trip. Leave the letter empty if it could not change.

setup.art: A diary page ruled into columns: day, where, kilometres, people, letter.
setup.caption: 1. Rule a diary page with five columns.

setup.art: A family at the dinner table adding one line to the diary each evening.
setup.caption: 2. Each evening add the day's engine trips.

setup.art: The finished page with some trips circled and a star next to the one change chosen.
setup.caption: 3. On the last day, circle the trips that could change and pick one to try.

flow.do: Rule the page into five columns and name each one. Ask your child to guess how many engine trips the family makes in one week. Write the guess at the top.
flow.say: For one week we write every trip that uses an engine. A trip counts if a scooter, car, auto or bus took us. What do you think the number will be? Why?
flow.kid: Rule five columns. Guess how many engine trips we make in a week.

ask.q: How many engine trips do you think we make in a week?
good: Any number with a reason, such as 'one every day for school'.
A guess is fine. The diary will check it.

flow.parent: Only the family's own trips go in the diary. It is not shared outside the home. Count a school bus or a shared auto as an engine trip too. Walking and cycling trips are not written.

flow.do: Each evening for five days, spend about 5 minutes. Add the day's engine trips to the page. Ask your child to say where you went, how far it was and how many people went. Guess the kilometres if you do not know.
flow.say: Which trips did we make today? Who was with us? About how far was it?
flow.kid: Add today's trips to the diary. Count the people who went.

ask.q: Could any trip today have been done another way?
good: A short trip could have been walked or cycled.
Two trips could have been joined into one.

flow.parent: Guess distances by walking time. A walk of 10 minutes is about 1 kilometre. Do not change what you normally do this week, so the diary shows what really happens. Do not make the child feel any trip was wrong.

flow.do: On day 7, add up the trips and the kilometres. Mark each trip with W, C, S or J if it could change. Count how many trips and kilometres could change. Choose one change to try next week and write it at the bottom.
flow.say: Let us add up the week. Which trips could we walk, cycle, share or join with another trip? Which one will we try?
flow.kid: Add up the trips. Mark the ones that could change. Pick one to try.

ask.q: Which trip would you change first, and why?
good: A short trip, because walking or cycling is easy.
One shared with a neighbour, because the car goes anyway.

ask.q: If every family changed one trip a week, what would happen to the fuel used by a city?
good: It would fall a lot, because there are so many families.
Any answer with a reason. A lot of small changes add up.

flow.parent: Be honest that some trips cannot change: a late night, heavy shopping, a sick person, no safe footpath. The aim is to see which can, and not to feel guilty about the rest. There is a rebound idea in the lesson: do not spend the saved fuel on extra driving.
flow.think: If your family does change one trip, who gains and who might lose?

challenges.title: Build a cart that carries 10 coins for 1 metre without a hand-push
challenges.context: This is an engineering problem. You build a small cart from a carton and bottle caps. Then you find a way to power it with wind or a stretched rubber band, so that it carries 10 coins along 1 metre.
challenges.problem: Make a cart that carries 10 one-rupee coins along a flat floor for 1 metre. After the start, nobody may touch or push it.
constraints: Build it from things at home: a small carton, bottle caps, straws, pencils, tape, paper and a rubber band.
It must carry all 10 coins and roll straight for 1 metre on a smooth floor.
Power can come from wind, a balloon or a stretched rubber band. A battery or a motor is not allowed.
After the start, hands stay off the cart.
materials: a small carton such as a toothpaste box or a tea box
4 bottle caps of the same size for wheels
2 drinking straws and 2 pencils for axles
sticky tape, a rubber band, a long balloon and some thick paper for a sail
a measuring tape or a ruler

setup.art: A small carton on four bottle-cap wheels with two pencils as axles running through straws taped under the carton.
setup.caption: 1. Build the cart body with wheels on pencil axles inside straw holders.

setup.art: The cart with 10 coins in a row inside and a paper sail on the front standing up.
setup.caption: 2. Load the coins. Try a sail pushed by a puff of breath from behind.

setup.art: The cart with a long balloon taped on top pointing backwards and a stretched rubber band at the front.
setup.caption: 3. Try a balloon jet and a stretched rubber band as other ways to give the push.

flow.do: A grown-up tapes two straws across the underside of the carton. Slide a pencil through each straw. Push a bottle cap on each pencil end. Check that the cart rolls straight when you push it with a finger.
flow.say: First, make a cart that rolls. Wheels turn on the pencil axles inside the straws. A wheel that is stuck will not roll.
flow.kid: Make a cart with four wheels. See if it rolls straight.
flow.parent: Pierce the bottle caps in the middle with a pointed tool, as an adult job. If the wheels rub on the carton, add a small gap with a bit of tape on each end of the pencil. A cart that wobbles will not go straight for 1 metre.

flow.do: Put the 10 coins in a line inside the carton. Give the cart one gentle push to see how far it rolls with the load. Mark where it stops.
flow.say: Now the cart carries the load. The push comes from your finger this time. How far does it go?
flow.kid: Load 10 coins. Give it one push. See how far it goes.

ask.q: Why does a loaded cart need more push than an empty one?
good: More weight needs more push to get going.
The same push moves a heavy thing less far.

flow.parent: This links with the balloon test. A heavier load needs a bigger push.

flow.do: Try one usual way to give the push. Stand a paper sail upright on the cart's front with tape. Blow from behind through a straw from 30 centimetres away. Or tape a long balloon on top, nozzle pointing backwards, blow it up and let go. Measure how far the cart goes.
flow.say: Try the usual ways. A sail catches your breath. A balloon pushes air backwards and the cart goes forwards.
flow.kid: Try a sail with your breath. Try a balloon on top of the cart.

ask.q: Which usual way carried the load farthest, and why?
good: Any honest answer from the test, with a reason.
The balloon, because it gives a longer push, or the sail on a big breath.

flow.do: Try one creative way. Stretch a rubber band between two bits of tape at the front of the cart. Hook it behind the cart's back edge and let it spring back to give the cart a kick. Or let the cart roll down a short slope made from a book. Measure each. Write what worked and what did not.
flow.say: Now invent your own way to push the cart. A stretched rubber band can store a push too. What will you try?
flow.kid: Try a rubber band or a slope. Write what worked.

ask.q: What was the best way to push the cart, and is there only one best way?
good: Answers will differ. Several ways can carry 10 coins for 1 metre.
The best way depends on what you have and what you want.

flow.parent: Do not rank one design as the right one. Each answer carries the load for some distance, and trade-offs such as time, cost and how easily it repeats are all worth talking about.

general: A paper sail on the cart, pushed from behind by breath or a hand fan.
A long balloon taped on top of the cart with its neck pointing backwards, as in the rocket test.
A rolling start down a slope made from a book, which gives the cart its push from gravity.
creative: A rubber band stretched between the carton and a fixed point, then let go so that it kicks the cart forwards.
A string tied to the cart and led over the table edge to a small weight, so that the falling weight pulls the cart.
A cart shaped like a boat with a large sail, to catch more wind on a smooth floor.
A cart pushed by a tiny second cart that rolls down a slope and bumps it.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own cart and your own way of pushing it. How much load can it carry for 1 metre? Is there one best way, or does the best way depend on what you want?

challenges.title: Plan the errands: do the day with the fewest engine kilometres
challenges.context: This is a planning problem. A family has five errands and one scooter. You draw a map and find a plan with fewer kilometres, less fuel and the same jobs done.
challenges.problem: A family has five jobs today: drop a child at school, buy vegetables, buy medicine, post a letter and visit a grandmother. Find a plan that does all five with the fewest engine kilometres.
constraints: Home is in the middle of the map. School is 2 kilometres north. The vegetable shop and the medicine shop are side by side, 1 kilometre east. The post office is 1 kilometre west. The grandmother lives 3 kilometres south.
Every job must be done today.
A walk of 1 kilometre takes about 15 minutes. The scooter can go anywhere.
The first plan is to go from home and back for each job on the scooter.
materials: a sheet of paper and a pencil
5 small coloured paper squares or beads to be the stops

setup.art: A hand-drawn map with home in the middle and school north, shops east, post office west and a house south, each with a distance in kilometres.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the map. Mark each place and write its distance from home.

setup.art: The same map with a loop drawn in one colour for the scooter and a dotted line for a walk.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one colour for scooter trips and a dotted line for walks.

flow.do: Draw the map. Write each distance on it. Add up the kilometres if the scooter goes out and back for each job. Remember that each trip is counted twice, there and back.
flow.say: First plan: a separate scooter trip for every job. How many kilometres is that, there and back, for all five?
flow.kid: Draw the map. Count the kilometres for five separate trips.

ask.q: How many kilometres does the first plan use?
good: 16 kilometres. School 4, vegetables 2, medicine 2, post 2, grandmother 6.
About 16. The check is 4 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 6.

flow.parent: Adding the shopping stops separately is the usual way. The count of 16 kilometres counts each trip there and back.

flow.do: Look for a better plan. Join the vegetable and medicine trips, because the shops are side by side. Walk to the post office. Count the scooter kilometres again.
flow.say: Can two jobs share one trip? Can any job be done on foot?
flow.kid: Find trips to join. Find a trip to walk. Count the kilometres again.

ask.q: Which jobs can be joined or walked, and how many kilometres does that save?
good: Vegetables and medicine in one trip, and the post office on foot. The scooter then goes 4 + 2 + 6 = 12 kilometres, which is 4 less.
Joining and walking saves 4 kilometres, a quarter of the fuel.

flow.parent: A walk of 1 kilometre each way takes 30 minutes in all. Talk about the time as well as the fuel.

flow.do: Look for creative ideas. Walk to the shops too. Ask the grandmother to come to you instead, or meet halfway. Ask a neighbour to take the child to school along with their own. Count the kilometres for your plan.
flow.say: Now think about other ways. Who else could go? Could someone come to you? Could the shops come to you?
flow.kid: Invent two more ways to save. Count the kilometres again.

ask.q: What other ways could the family save fuel?
good: Share the school trip with a neighbour, walk to the shops, or ask the grandmother to visit.
Any plan with a reason, and a count of the kilometres.

ask.q: What would be lost with each plan, and what would be gained?
good: Walking takes more time and gives a walk. Sharing needs a neighbour.
Each plan trades time, money and fuel.

flow.parent: There is no single right plan. A plan that saves the most fuel may take the most time. Let the child weigh up the trade-offs.
flow.think: What would make you choose the fastest plan, and what would make you choose the plan that uses the least fuel?

general: Join the vegetable shop and the medicine shop into one trip, since they are side by side.
Walk to the post office, 1 kilometre away.
Do the school drop and come straight back, with no extra trips.
creative: Share the school trip with a neighbour who goes the same way, so one scooter takes two children.
Ask the grandmother to meet the family halfway, or to come to the house.
Walk to the shops too, and carry the shopping home in a bag.
Ask a shop to deliver the medicine along with its other deliveries.
challenges.your_turn: Draw the map of your own errands for one day. Find a plan that uses fewer engine kilometres. Which plan would your family really choose?

games.title: Back to the Sun: a family-of-cards game with 20 cards
games.players: 2 to 4 players. A parent and a child are enough.
games.context: In this card game you collect the four cards of each family, from a vehicle back to the sunlight that first gave its push. Asking for cards makes you think about where each push comes from.

setup.art: Twenty small cards cut out from a printed sheet and laid face down in a pile on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 20 cards and shuffle them.

setup.art: Two players holding five cards each with a draw pile between them.
setup.caption: 2. Deal 5 cards each for two players, or 4 each for four. Put the rest face down.

setup.art: One finished family laid in a row: a cycle, legs, breakfast and a sunlit rice plant.
setup.caption: 3. Lay a finished family in a line from the vehicle to the sunlight.

printables.title: 20 cards: five families of four, from a vehicle back to the Sun
items: Cycle family: the cycle rolling down the road
Cycle family: your leg muscles turning the pedals
Cycle family: your breakfast of idli and sambar, stored in your body
Cycle family: sunlight falling on the rice and lentil plants that made the food
Bullock cart family: the bullock cart rolling along a village road
Bullock cart family: the bullock's muscles pulling the cart
Bullock cart family: the grass and grain that the bullock eats
Bullock cart family: sunlight falling on the grass and grain fields
Diesel bus family: the bus rolling along the highway
Diesel bus family: diesel burning inside the bus engine
Diesel bus family: oil under the ground, made of tiny sea beings buried long ago
Diesel bus family: sunlight falling on a warm sea millions of years ago
Electric scooter family: the electric scooter humming down the street
Electric scooter family: the scooter's battery, filled up at the wall
Electric scooter family: coal burning in a power station to make that electricity
Electric scooter family: sunlight falling on forests of long ago that became coal
Sailing boat family: a wooden boat crossing the sea
Sailing boat family: the wind pressing on the boat's sail
Sailing boat family: air that moves because the Sun warms some places more than others
Sailing boat family: sunlight falling on the land and the sea

printables.title: Score sheet to copy by hand: one row for each family and a column for each player
items: Cycle family: put a tick for the player who laid it down, and a star for the right order.
Bullock cart family: put a tick for the player who laid it down, and a star for the right order.
Diesel bus family: put a tick for the player who laid it down, and a star for the right order.
Electric scooter family: put a tick for the player who laid it down, and a star for the right order.
Sailing boat family: put a tick for the player who laid it down, and a star for the right order.

rules: There are five families of four cards. Each family begins with a vehicle and ends with the sunlight that first gave the push.
Deal 5 cards to each player for two players, or 4 cards each for three or four players. Put the rest face down as the draw pile.
On your turn, ask one player for a card from a family you already hold. For example, 'Do you have the cycle's breakfast card?' You must hold at least one card of that family.
If they have it, they give it to you and you ask again. If they do not, you draw one card. If you draw the card you asked for, show it and take another turn. Otherwise your turn ends.
When you hold all four cards of a family, lay them in a row on the table. Put the vehicle on the left and the sunlight on the right, and say how each step gives its push to the next.
Score one point for each family you lay down. Score one more point, a star, if the other player agrees that your order goes the right way, from vehicle to sunlight, with no help.
If your hand is empty, draw one card. If the draw pile is empty, you can only ask other players.
The game ends when all five families are laid down. The player with most points wins. If points are equal, you share the win.
Playing alone, lay out all 20 cards face up and sort them into five rows, from vehicle to sunlight. Then check your rows with a parent.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards from the printed sheet. Shuffle them. Read the five family names out loud: cycle, bullock cart, diesel bus, electric scooter, sailing boat.
flow.say: There are five families of cards. Each family has a vehicle and the things that give it a push, all the way back to the Sun.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read the five families out loud.
flow.parent: Cutting is for the grown-up if the child is under 8. Keep the cards in a small envelope for another day.

flow.do: Deal the cards and play. Take turns asking for cards. When a family is complete, the player lays it in a row. Then the player says how each card gives its push to the next.
flow.say: Ask for a card from a family you hold. When you have all four, lay them in a line and tell us the story from the vehicle back to the Sun.
flow.kid: Ask for a card. Lay a family in a row when you have all four.

ask.q: What gave the push to the cycle, and what gave the push to the food?
good: Leg muscles gave the push, and breakfast gave energy to the muscles. The plants made the food from sunlight.
The food. The food came from plants, and plants took the energy from the Sun.

flow.parent: If the cards in a row are in the wrong order, ask what each card gives to the next one. Ask this gently, as a question, before saying the order is wrong.

flow.do: Look at the five rows. Ask which family is different from the others, and why. Ask the big question.
flow.say: Look at all five rows. They all end in sunlight. Is there any vehicle that does not run on the Sun?
flow.kid: Look at the five rows. Where does each one end?

ask.q: Is there any vehicle in the game that does not run on the Sun?
good: No. Each one goes back to the Sun, some after a short time and some after millions of years.
Every row ends with sunlight, but oil and coal are far older than food or wind.

ask.q: Which sunlight is the oldest?
good: The sunlight in the oil, and in the coal.
The sea and forests of long ago.

flow.parent: A solar panel turns sunlight into electricity directly. A few vehicles, such as nuclear-powered ships, use a source that is not sunlight at all. That is a good question to leave open.
flow.think: Can you think of any vehicle that would not need the Sun at all?

games.title: Road bingo: 12 things to spot on a walk or a bus ride
games.context: Here you spot things on the road that link to what powers vehicles. Spotting them makes you notice what is around you every day.

setup.art: A bingo sheet with twelve squares, each with a small picture, held on a clipboard by a child on a footpath.
setup.caption: 1. Draw or print the bingo sheet with twelve squares.

setup.art: A child and parent walking on a footpath with a pencil to tick off squares.
setup.caption: 2. Walk with a grown-up and tick each square when you see it.

printables.title: 12 bingo squares: things to spot on the road
items: a vehicle that burns petrol, such as a scooter or a car
a vehicle that burns diesel, such as a bus or a lorry
the letters CNG on a vehicle or a sign
a quiet vehicle that may run on a battery
a cycle
an animal pulling or carrying something
a vehicle with four or more people in it
a car with only one person in it
a vehicle with its engine running while it waits
a petrol pump
people walking on a footpath
people waiting at a bus stop

rules: Each player has a copy of the 12 squares. You can copy them by hand onto paper in a 4 by 3 grid.
Walk or ride with a grown-up. Stay on the footpath or on your seat.
When you see a square, call it out. The first player to call it ticks it. Other players cannot tick that one. Two players who call together both tick.
After 15 minutes, count your ticks. The player with the most wins. If you play alone, try to tick all 12.
After the game, choose two ticked squares and say what gave each vehicle its push.

flow.do: Copy the 12 squares onto a sheet of paper in a grid of 4 across and 3 down. Read the squares to your child.
flow.say: We will spot twelve things on our walk. Read the squares. Which one will be hardest to find?
flow.kid: Copy the squares. Read each one out loud.
flow.parent: A pencil and a clipboard or hard book help. A bus ride works as well as a walk.

flow.do: Go for a walk or a bus ride with your child. Call out and tick each square. Stay on the footpath.
flow.say: Spot as many as you can. Call it out when you see one. The first to call gets the tick.
flow.kid: Spot the squares. Call each one out. Tick it.

ask.q: Which square was hardest to find, and why?
good: A quiet battery vehicle or a CNG sign, because there are fewer of them.
Any answer, with a reason from what they saw.

flow.parent: Keep close to your child near roads. If nothing is quiet enough to hear, check any vehicle with a green number plate. A green plate marks an electric vehicle in India.

flow.do: Count the ticks. Choose two squares and ask what gave each vehicle its push and where that push came from.
flow.say: Pick two squares. What gave each vehicle its push?
flow.kid: Choose two ticked squares. Say what pushed each vehicle.

ask.q: What pushed the vehicles you found, and where did that push come from?
good: Petrol, diesel, CNG or a battery, and before that old sunlight or a power station.
Legs on the cycle, from food, from the Sun.

worksheets.title: What pushes a vehicle? (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks that you can say what makes different vehicles go and what a fuel is, and that you can give ways to save fuel.

items.p: What does a cycle use in place of petrol from a pump?
opts: The rider's muscles, run on food
items.why: A cycle runs on the rider's muscles, and muscles run on food. A cycle has no engine, no tank and no battery.

items.p: A muscle's fuel is ____.
items.why: Muscles get their energy from the food we eat. A breakfast of idli moves the legs that push the pedals.

items.p: Match each vehicle to what makes it go.
pairs: Green and yellow auto in Delhi
items.why: Each vehicle gets its push from a different source. A cycle uses muscles, a cart uses the bullocks, a bus burns diesel, a scooter uses a battery and the auto burns CNG.

items.p: Sort each vehicle by how it gets its push.
cats: Does not burn fuel in an engine
items: diesel bus
Burns fuel in an engine
cycle
Does not burn fuel in an engine
electric scooter
Does not burn fuel in an engine
CNG auto
Burns fuel in an engine
bullock cart
Does not burn fuel in an engine
petrol scooter
Burns fuel in an engine
items.why: An engine burns a fuel to make hot gas that pushes a piston. A cycle, a cart and an electric scooter get their push in other ways.

items.p: Most petrol is made from the bones of dinosaurs.
items.why: False. Most oil came from tiny floating sea beings that sank into the mud of warm seas. Their remains were squeezed and heated for millions of years.

items.p: Put these in order, from the Sun to the moving cycle.
a: Your leg muscles turning the pedals
items.why: The Sun's light is caught by the plant. The plant's rice becomes breakfast. Your body keeps the energy. Your muscles use it to push the pedals, and the cycle rolls.

items.p: Write two ways your family could save petrol or diesel this week.
items.a: Two ideas, each with a reason. For example, walk or cycle to a nearby shop, join two errands, share a ride, switch off at a long wait or pump up the tyres.
items.why: Fuel is saved by not using an engine, by sharing, and by careful driving. A strong answer says why the idea saves fuel.

items.p: Draw a village road and a city road. Put one vehicle on each and label its push.
items.a: A village road with a cycle, a tractor or a bullock cart, and a city road with a bus, a car or a metro. Each is labelled with legs, bullocks, diesel, petrol or electricity.
items.why: The two places have different traffic. A strong drawing shows that the village has fewer vehicles, with many cycles and animals, and the city has crowds of vehicles with engines.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Petrol, diesel, CNG, electricity.
items.a: Electricity, because it is not burned in the vehicle. Petrol, diesel and CNG are burned in an engine.
items.why: Fuels give out heat when they burn. Electricity from a battery turns a motor and nothing burns inside the vehicle.

items.p: Two ways to go to a shop 2 kilometres away.

views.says: The scooter is quick. I can carry a heavy bag and I am there in minutes.
My cycle burns no fuel, costs nothing to run and carries me there on very little energy.

items.ask: Which would you choose for a 2 kilometre trip with a heavy bag, and what would change your mind?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks one and says what would change its mind, such as a heavy bag, rain or the time.
items.why: Each way has good points. The scooter is quick and carries a heavy bag. The cycle burns no fuel and uses little energy of your own.

worksheets.title: Fuels, sharing and electric vehicles (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to work out how much travel a litre of fuel gives. It also asks you to compare ways of saving and to think about both sides of electric vehicles.

items.p: Why does a cycle use less energy than walking for the same distance?
opts: A cycle has a small engine
The saddle holds you up and the wheels roll
items.why: When you walk, your legs lift your body at every step. On a cycle the saddle holds you up and the wheels roll, so your legs only turn the pedals.

items.p: An electric scooter makes no carbon dioxide anywhere.
items.why: False. The scooter gives out none on the road. The electricity may come from a power station that burns coal, and making the battery also takes energy.

items.p: A van takes 8 people 10 kilometres on one litre. How many kilometres of travel is that for all 8 together?
items.why: 8 people times 10 kilometres is 80 kilometres of travel from one litre.

items.p: Burning one litre of petrol makes about ____ kilograms of carbon dioxide.
items.why: The petrol joins with oxygen from the air. The new gas weighs more than the petrol, about 2.3 kilograms for one litre.

items.p: Match each way of saving fuel to why it works.
pairs: Switch off at a railway gate
The engine stops burning fuel while standing still
Do three errands in one outing
items.why: Each idea cuts fuel in a different way. Some stop the engine burning when it is standing still, some cut rubbing, and some share or join trips.

items.p: Put these in order, from the least fuel for each person to the most.
a: Bus with 50 people, 4 kilometres on a litre
Scooter with 2 people, 45 kilometres on a litre
Car with 4 people, 15 kilometres on a litre
Car with 1 person, 15 kilometres on a litre
items.why: Multiply people by kilometres on a litre. The bus gives 200, the scooter with 2 gives 90, the car with 4 gives 60 and the car alone gives 15. A bigger number means less fuel for each person.

items.p: Why do wider roads often fill up with vehicles again?
items.a: A wider road makes driving easier, so extra people choose to drive and extra vehicles come. The extra space fills up and the jam returns.
items.why: More road space can mean more driving. A strong answer says that people change what they do when the road changes.

items.p: Write one good thing and one problem about electric scooters.
items.a: A good thing, such as no exhaust smoke on the street, a quiet motor or little wasted energy. A problem, such as electricity from coal, mining for battery metals or the cost.
items.why: Electric scooters help in some ways and not in others. A strong answer gives both and says why.

items.p: Sort each one by the kind of place where you see it most.
items: a metro train overhead
Usually city traffic
a bullock cart
Usually village traffic
a flyover over a crossing
Usually city traffic
a bus that comes four times a day
Usually village traffic
a traffic jam at six o'clock
Usually city traffic
buffaloes crossing the road
Usually village traffic
items.why: A city has many vehicles in little space, with signals and flyovers. A village has fewer vehicles, with more cycles, tractors and animal carts.

items.p: Who should get more of a city road?

views.who: A child who walks to school (an imagined view)
views.says: The footpath is narrow and broken. I need a wide, safe path.
I need space to drive to work, or I will be late for my job.

items.ask: How could the road be shared so that both of them are better off?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says who the road is for, and how it could be shared.
items.why: Both people have a real need. About one in three Indian workers walk or cycle to work, and most road space still goes to motor vehicles.

worksheets.title: Old sunlight, rebound and the future (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks harder questions. Why does saving fuel not always save fuel? How are food and fuel alike? What may vehicles run on in future?

items.p: Engines now waste less fuel, yet the world burns more. Which idea explains it?
opts: Cheaper driving can lead to more driving
items.why: When a vehicle costs less to run, people tend to drive more and buy bigger vehicles. This is called the rebound effect. William Jevons noticed it with coal in 1865.

items.p: Running a petrol vehicle is running on very old sunlight.
items.why: True. Tiny sea beings caught sunlight millions of years ago. Their remains became oil, and the oil holds that energy.

items.p: Ants on a crowded trail avoid jams by ____ down.
items.why: Ants adjust their speed and stop entering a crowded trail. Experiments in 2019 found this. Scientists are still working out the exact rules.

items.p: A car that stands with its engine running burns half a litre in one hour. How many litres in 4 hours?
items.why: Half a litre each hour for 4 hours is 4 halves, which makes 2 litres.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Petrol, diesel, coal, ethanol.
items.a: Ethanol, because it is made from plants grown recently. The others are fossil fuels, made from living beings of millions of years ago.
items.why: Ethanol comes from sugarcane or maize that grew this year, and new plants can be grown. Fossil fuels took millions of years to form.

items.p: Petrol and breakfast both hold sunlight. How are they different?
items.a: Breakfast holds sunlight from a few months ago and petrol holds sunlight from millions of years ago. People use petrol far faster than it forms, while crops can be grown again.
items.why: Both store energy first caught from the Sun. The difference is the age, and how fast we use them compared with how fast they are made.

items.p: A bullock pulls a cart all day. Write three things a kind owner should do.
items.a: Give shade and water, let the bullock rest in the midday heat, keep the load light and stop at the end of a working day. A bullock tires, feels heat and needs rest.
items.why: A working animal is a living being who tires, thirsts and feels heat. Indian rules from 1965 limit work to nine hours and call for rest in the heat.

items.p: Draw a chain from the Sun to an electric scooter that is charged from a coal power station.
items.a: Sunlight on a forest of long ago, coal, a power station, a wire, a battery and the scooter, each with an arrow.
items.why: The energy in coal was first sunlight caught by trees of long ago. The power station burns the coal to make electricity, and the battery stores it.

items.p: A friend says CNG made Delhi's air clean for ever. Which reply is best?
opts: Yes, it made the air clean for ever
It helped at first, but the smoke came back
No, CNG is the same as diesel
CNG caused all of Delhi's smoke
items.why: CNG cut black smoke at first. Later there were many more vehicles, and dust, industry and burning, so the air got bad again. One change of fuel does not settle the matter.

items.p: What should most vehicles run on in fifty years?

views.who: Car makers who build hydrogen vehicles, such as Toyota and Hyundai
views.says: Hydrogen fills in minutes and carries a lorry far with no heavy battery. It gives only water.
Charging a battery wastes about three times less energy than making hydrogen, and charging points already exist.

items.ask: What would you want to find out before you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer gives a reason for each choice and says what could change it.
items.why: Nobody knows yet. Batteries are ahead for scooters and cars. Hydrogen may suit lorries, but making it takes a lot of electricity.

quiz.p: A bullock cart rolls along a road. What gives it the push?
opts: The bullocks' muscles, run on grass and grain
quiz.why: The wheels roll, but they do not push. The push comes from the bullocks' muscles, and the muscles run on the food they eat. If you chose the wheels, try asking what turns them.

quiz.p: Which of these needs no fuel tank and no battery?
quiz.why: A cycle is pushed by the rider's muscles, which run on food. The bus burns diesel, the auto burns CNG and the scooter needs a battery.

opts: A liquid kept in a tank
A thing that makes a loud noise
Something that gives out heat when it burns
quiz.why: A fuel is anything that gives out heat when it burns. Many fuels are liquids, but CNG is a gas and coal is a solid rock, so 'a liquid' is not the whole answer.

quiz.p: Which of these is a gas that is squeezed into a cylinder?
quiz.why: CNG is natural gas squeezed into a strong cylinder. Petrol and diesel are liquids, and coal is a hard black rock.

quiz.p: What was petrol mostly made from?
opts: Tiny sea beings of long ago, buried and squeezed
quiz.why: Millions of years ago tiny floating beings died and sank into the mud of warm seas. Heat and squeezing turned their remains into oil. Dinosaurs were not the main source.

quiz.p: Why will petrol and diesel not last for ever?
opts: They took millions of years to form
The Sun makes a little more each year
quiz.why: The oil took millions of years to form and people are using much of it in little more than a hundred. It is not being made again at anything like the speed we burn it.

quiz.p: An electric scooter makes no smoke. Why might some smoke still be made?
opts: Its battery is full of smoke
Coal may be burned at a power station to make its electricity
quiz.why: The scooter itself gives out no exhaust. But in India most electricity still comes from burning coal, so some smoke has only moved to a chimney far away.

quiz.p: What does an electric scooter have in place of a tank and an engine?
quiz.why: The battery stores electricity and the motor uses magnets to turn it into the spinning of the wheel. Nothing is burned inside the scooter.

quiz.p: A driver waits 3 minutes at a closed railway gate. What saves fuel?
opts: Press the pedal now and then
Keep it running so it will not stall
quiz.why: A running engine burns fuel even when the vehicle goes nowhere. Switching it off for a wait of a minute or more saves fuel, and a modern engine starts again easily.

quiz.p: A shop is 500 metres from home. Which way saves the most fuel?
opts: Take the scooter with a friend
Drive, and keep the engine running
Go twice, once for each thing
quiz.why: Walking or cycling burns no fuel at all. Sharing helps, but the best saving is not to use an engine for a short trip.

quiz.p: Which is more likely on a village road than at a city crossing?
opts: Hundreds of vehicles in five minutes
A long jam at six o'clock
A bullock cart or a tractor
quiz.why: A village road has fewer vehicles. It has more cycles, walkers, tractors and animal carts. A metro, a jam and hundreds of vehicles belong to a city.

quiz.p: A car carries 1 person and a bus carries 50. Which uses less fuel for each person?
opts: The bus, because 50 people share its fuel
The car, because it burns less
quiz.why: The bus burns more, but it shares the fuel between 50 people. One litre carries the bus 4 kilometres, which is 200 kilometres of travel altogether, and carries the car only 15.

quiz.p: Why do we try each amount of air three times in the balloon test?
opts: One try could be a fluke
quiz.why: A single try could be lucky or unlucky. Three tries show if the result happens again, and the middle value is less likely to be a fluke.

quiz.p: 2 breaths sent a balloon 120 centimetres and 4 breaths sent it 200. What can you say?
opts: Double the air gave exactly double the distance
More air went farther, but not double
quiz.why: Double 120 is 240, but the balloon went only 200. More air gave a longer trip, but some of the push was lost to rubbing and to pushing air aside.

maths.problem: A balloon rocket went 3 ruler lengths with 2 breaths and 5 ruler lengths with 4 breaths. If double the air gave double the distance, how far would 4 breaths have gone? How many ruler lengths short was it?
maths.answer: 6 ruler lengths. It was 1 ruler length short.
maths.explain: Double 3 is 3 + 3 = 6. The balloon went 5, and 6 − 5 = 1 ruler length less.
maths.why_maths: Doubling shows what a perfect result would be. The gap between that and the real result tells us that some push was lost on the way.

maths.problem: One litre takes a bus 4 kilometres. The bus carries 50 people. How many kilometres of travel does one litre give for all of them? Do the same for a car with 4 people that goes 15 kilometres on a litre. Which is bigger?
maths.answer: Bus 200 kilometres, car 60 kilometres. The bus is bigger.
maths.explain: The bus is 50 groups of 4 kilometres, which is 200. The car is 4 groups of 15 kilometres, which is 60. 200 is more than 60.
maths.why_maths: Fuel used for each person cannot be seen by looking at the vehicle. Equal groups show how many people share each litre.

maths.problem: A family goes to the market 3 times a week. Each trip is 2 kilometres there and 2 kilometres back. How many kilometres is that in a week? How many if they join two trips into one?
maths.answer: 12 kilometres, and 8 kilometres with joined trips.
maths.explain: Each trip is 2 + 2 = 4 kilometres. 3 trips are 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. With only 2 trips it is 4 + 4 = 8, which is 4 kilometres less.
maths.why_maths: Adding the same trip again and again shows how many kilometres a habit adds up to, and how a small change cuts it.

maths.problem: From a window a child counts 12 scooters, 9 cars, 6 autos, 3 cycles and 2 buses in five minutes. How many of them have engines? How many more scooters than cycles were there? Which row is longest?
maths.answer: 29 have engines. 9 more scooters than cycles. Scooters are the longest row.
maths.explain: Add the ones with engines: 12 + 9 + 6 + 2 = 29. Cycles have no engine. 12 − 3 = 9. 12 is the biggest number.
maths.why_maths: A tally turns what you see on a road into numbers that you can add, subtract and compare.

maths.problem: A car goes 15 kilometres on one litre. How many litres does it use to go 45 kilometres? How many to go 90 kilometres?
maths.explain: 45 is 3 groups of 15, so 3 litres. 90 is 6 groups of 15, so 6 litres. Doubling the distance doubles the litres.
maths.why_maths: Fuel use grows in steps with the distance. Counting groups of 15 shows that a trip twice as long needs twice the fuel.

applications: At a petrol pump, read the signs on each pump: petrol, diesel or CNG. Watch which vehicles pull up to which pump, and notice that a scooter and a bus drink different fuels.
Look at the underside of a green and yellow auto in Delhi, Mumbai or Pune, and find the tall cylinder at the back. That cylinder holds CNG, the squeezed natural gas that the engine burns.
A school bus carries thirty children to school on one tank. Count the children in your street who go to the same school. That is how many vehicles one bus takes off the road.
The dabbawalas of Mumbai carry about two lakh lunch boxes each day by cycle, handcart and train, and almost no fuel is burned on the way. Look at how they use legs and rails.
A cycle rickshaw driver in Kolkata or Mathura pedals three passengers along. Watch his legs on a slope, and notice how a rider uses muscle power to move more than his own weight.
At a railway gate in your town, count the engines that stay on while the train goes by. A driver who switches off for a minute or more saves fuel that would burn for nothing.

A metro train such as the Chennai Metro or the Kochi Metro runs on electricity and carries hundreds of people at once. Next time you ride it, count the people in one coach and think of how many vehicles they would need on a road.

spotted.text: On the way to school, look at the back of every scooter and car. Find a sticker or a plate that shows petrol, diesel, CNG or electric. Count how many of each you see.
spotted.art: A row of scooters at a signal with stickers and green number plates on a few of them.

spotted.text: Stand on the footpath at a signal, with a grown-up, and watch the exhaust pipes. Which vehicles are puffing smoke, and which are silent while waiting?
spotted.art: A line of vehicles at a red signal, some with exhaust puffs and some with none.

spotted.text: Find a bullock cart, a tractor or a handcart near your home or on a trip. Ask what gives it its push, and look at the wheels and the axle.
spotted.art: A bullock cart on a village road with the wheel and axle drawn larger beside it.

spotted.text: At the next petrol pump, find the number on the pump that shows the price for one litre. Ask how much one litre costs and how far it could take a scooter.
spotted.art: A petrol pump display with a number for litres and a number for rupees.

spotted.text: Look at the tyres of a parked scooter and a parked bus. Which tyre looks soft and which looks hard? A soft tyre rubs more on the road.
spotted.art: A parked scooter with a soft front tyre next to a bus with a firm tyre.

spotted.text: At a bus stop, look at how many people get on one bus. Ask how many cars it would take to carry the same people, if each car carried only the driver.
spotted.art: A bus with many passengers climbing in, with a row of empty-looking cars drawn faintly behind.

spotted.text: On a walk, count the footpaths. Are they wide and clear for people, or narrow and blocked? Look at who is walking in the road instead.
spotted.art: A narrow footpath blocked by parked scooters, with a child walking in the road beside it.

ask_kids: When you go to school, what gives your vehicle its push? What does that push come from before it was a fuel?
What is the farthest you have ever walked? What did your body use to get you there?
If a bullock could talk, what would she or he ask you for after a day of pulling a cart?
Imagine all the vehicles on your street stopped for one day. What would you notice? What would still work?
Which trip does your family make by an engine that you think you could make another way? What would change if you did?
If you could invent a new way to move people, with no fuel and no smoke, what would it use?
Why do you think a bus feels slow but uses less fuel for each person than a car?
A pump gives us petrol in a minute. The oil took millions of years to make. What do you think about that?

warmup.q: What does a cycle use to move, in place of a fuel tank?
warmup.a: The rider's muscles, which run on food.
Something that gives out heat when it burns.

warmup.q: Name three fuels that vehicles burn.
warmup.a: Petrol, diesel and CNG are three. Coal and wood are fuels too.

warmup.q: What is the first thing a toy car needs before it moves?
True or false: an electric scooter has an engine that burns petrol.
warmup.a: False. It has a battery and a motor.

warmup.q: Where does the energy in your breakfast first come from?
warmup.a: The Sun. Plants catch sunlight and make the food.

warmup.q: Which has more vehicles in five minutes, a city crossing or a village road?
Name one way to save petrol.
warmup.a: Walk or cycle short trips, share a ride, join two trips, or switch off the engine when waiting.

quiz: A cycle needs a fuel tank.
A cycle has no tank. The rider's muscles push the pedals, and the muscles run on food.
A bus carries many people, so each person can use less fuel than in a car.
A bus burns more fuel than a car, but it shares it among many people.
Petrol comes from tiny sea beings of long ago.
Their remains were buried, squeezed and heated for millions of years until they became oil.
An electric scooter gives out smoke from a pipe.
An electric scooter has no exhaust pipe. Smoke may be made at a power station far away.
Walking to a nearby shop saves petrol.
A walk uses no fuel from a pump at all.
